articles.title: Widespread selection of antibiotic resistance within hospital sewers
articles.titleEn: Widespread selection of antibiotic resistance within hospital sewers
articles.abstract: Environmental microbiomes are sources of diverse antibiotic resistance determinants that can be mobilized and transferred to human pathogens under a selection pressure from antibiotics. Hospital sewers contain more antibiotics than most environments and are thus increasingly recognised as potential arenas for resistance evolution. However, it is unknown if resistance selection occurs there and what the drivers are. Here we show selection of antibiotic-resistant bacteria within Swedish hospital sewers. Evidence include; consistent selection of multiple resistances in Escherichia coli exposed to filtered wastewater from ten hospitals, but not to corresponding municipal wastewaters; in-situ enrichment of resistant over sensitive E. coli from wastewater to sewer biofilms at hospitals, but not at municipal sites; and higher resistance in bacteria collected from hospital sewers than from municipal sites as assessed by culturing and metagenomics. Evidence for drivers includes complete rescue of sensitive E. coli by addition of resistance genes to fluoroquinolones and β-lactams, and cellular effects typical for β-lactams. Measured concentrations by liquid-chromatography-tandem-mass-spectrometry compared to selective thresholds identify ciprofloxacin and cefotaxime as principal selective agents. Antibiotic concentrations and use data allow extrapolation of risks beyond Sweden. Given the absence of detectable selection at municipal sites, mitigations of risks in hospital sewers should be prioritized.

articles.title: Global socio-economic resilience to disasters
articles.titleEn: Global socio-economic resilience to disasters
articles.abstract: Most disaster risk assessments use asset damages as their central metric, often neglecting distributional impacts and affected people’s coping and recovery capacity. To address this, the concepts of well-being losses and socio-economic resilience—the ability to experience asset damages without a decline in well-being—have been proposed. Here we provide a global picture of well-being losses and socio-economic resilience using microsimulations. Across 132 countries, 1 dollar in damages causes well-being losses equivalent to a 2-dollar uniform national consumption drop. The poorest populations incur only 9% of damages but 33% of well-being losses. A 10% higher gross domestic product per capita is associated with a 1 percentage point resilience increase. Low-income countries experience 72% greater well-being losses per dollar of damages and need 92% longer to recover than high-income countries. Socio-economic and financial interventions can complement asset-focused policies, and targeting low-income populations usually yields higher well-being returns. Our results offer a starting point for a discussion on more comprehensive risk metrics and risk management policies for sustainable development.

articles.title: Impact of Spatial Variability in Root‐Zone Storage Deficit on Runoff Generation
articles.titleEn: Impact of Spatial Variability in Root‐Zone Storage Deficit on Runoff Generation
articles.abstract: The root zone stores water for plants and is a source of drainage that drives runoff. Previous work demonstrated that significant drainage to drive runoff is predicated on the replenishment of the root‐zone moisture deficit. A method for quantifying the root‐zone storage deficit (hereafter, “the deficit”) based on a running balance of water entering the root zone via rainfall and snowmelt and water leaving the root zone via evapotranspiration has been gaining popularity over the past decade. Distributed deficit data have been shown to be useful for improving runoff predictions at the basin scale, but there is opportunity to further explore variability in deficit and runoff dynamics throughout basins and how this heterogeneity plays a role in catchment behavior. Here we calculate deficits at 4 km resolution in a set of basins across the Sierra Nevada in California. We demonstrate that deficits can vary substantially across a catchment, with deficit growth and replenishment occurring at different times and with different magnitudes in different locations. More importantly, heterogeneity in pixel deficits results in different timing and amount of inferred runoff from different parts of the catchment, differences that persist when pixel calculations are aggregated to the catchment scale. Our findings reveal that, even using this simple mass balance approach, it is important to account for spatially variable behavior in order to accurately capture the magnitude of runoff at the catchment scale and that deficit tracking approaches may contribute to quantifying runoff in ungauged basins.

articles.title: Vegetation increasingly controlled by atmospheric dryness rather than soil moisture
articles.titleEn: Vegetation increasingly controlled by atmospheric dryness rather than soil moisture
articles.abstract: Terrestrial vegetation regulates global carbon cycling and climate through responses to water availability. Yet, it remains unclear whether soil moisture (SM) or atmospheric dryness (vapour pressure deficit, VPD) dominates vegetation responses and, more critically, how their relative influence changes over time, limiting predictions of ecosystem–climate feedback under warming. Here we analyse satellite-derived vegetation variability over the past four decades using an explainable artificial intelligence framework that disentangles nonlinear hydroclimatic driver contributions. We show SM dominates vegetation variability in most regions. However, VPD influence has strengthened while SM influence has weakened over time. These changes highlight an asymmetric transition with more SM-dominated ecosystems shifting towards increasing VPD control than vice versa. Changes in the mean and variability of SM and VPD drive this transition by altering plant water-stress responses. Continued warming will probably intensify this pattern as rising VPD and more frequent extreme events strengthen atmospheric constraints on vegetation.

articles.title: A single-molecule spin–photon interface
articles.titleEn: A single-molecule spin–photon interface
articles.abstract: Optical interfaces that connect long-lived spin qubits to photons are a central requirement for quantum networking and distributed quantum information processing. At present, solid-state atomic defects are leading candidates because of their inherent spin and optical coherence 1,2 . Building on these advancements, synthetically tailored molecular systems represent a fundamental change in the field, using precise atomic control and consistent bottom-up assembly 3,4 . However, a molecular platform that concurrently satisfies the demands of a robust spin–photon interface—namely, the combination of bright fluorescence, high spectral stability and long ground-state spin lifetimes—has yet to be realized at the single-molecule level. Here we show that a triplet ground-state carbene molecule, embedded within a structurally matched host crystal, functions as a robust spin–photon interface with single-molecule addressability. The system exhibits narrow ZPLs, spectral stability over more than an hour, spin-selective optical transitions and single-molecule optically detected magnetic resonance. Coherent control yields millisecond-scale dynamical-decoupling coherence and tens-of-milliseconds spin relaxation at a temperature of 4.5 K. These results establish molecular qubits as a viable platform for single-emitter quantum optics 5,6 while preserving the advantages of bottom-up chemical design 7 and processable materials 8–10 .

articles.title: MCT1-dependent mitochondrial lactate import sustains cardiac metabolism
articles.titleEn: MCT1-dependent mitochondrial lactate import sustains cardiac metabolism
articles.abstract: The heart possesses a dynamic capacity to oxidize a variety of fuels, including glucose and lactate, to meet its energetic demands under diverse dietary, exertion and injury stressors 1 . Oxidation of carbohydrate substrates is thought to converge on the cytosolic generation of pyruvate, which is transported by the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier (MPC) for entry into the tricarboxylic acid cycle 2 . Here we find that glucose-derived carbon is oxidized in mouse myocardium even when the MPC is genetically ablated. Using genetic and pharmacological tools, we demonstrate that lactate monocarboxylate transporter 1 (MCT1, encoded by Slc16a1 ) is required for the oxidation of glucose carbon by MPC-deficient myocardium. We further observe that MCT1, traditionally localized to the plasma membrane, also resides in the inner mitochondrial membrane of mouse and human cardiomyocytes. Together with matrix-localized LDHB, MCT1 enables mitochondrial lactate conversion to pyruvate and NADH, directly fueling the electron transport chain. Loss of MCT1 impairs lactate oxidation, disrupts metabolic flexibility and accelerates the development of heart failure with increased mortality after hyperactivation of the neurohormonal axis or ischemia–reperfusion injury. Thus, the existence of a parallel lactate-based pathway for carbohydrate oxidation can sustain cardiac energetics and maintain myocardial structure and function under diverse stress conditions.

Here we find that glucose-derived carbon is oxidized in mouse myocardium even when the MPC is genetically ablated. Using genetic and pharmacological tools, we demonstrate that lactate monocarboxylate transporter 1 (MCT1, encoded by Slc16a1 ) is required for the oxidation of glucose carbon by MPC-deficient myocardium. We further observe that MCT1, traditionally localized to the plasma membrane, also resides in the inner mitochondrial membrane of mouse and human cardiomyocytes. Together with matrix-localized LDHB, MCT1 enables mitochondrial lactate conversion to pyruvate and NADH, directly fueling the electron transport chain. Loss of MCT1 impairs lactate oxidation, disrupts metabolic flexibility and accelerates the development of heart failure with increased mortality after hyperactivation of the neurohormonal axis or ischemia–reperfusion injury. Thus, the existence of a parallel lactate-based pathway for carbohydrate oxidation can sustain cardiac energetics and maintain myocardial structure and function under diverse stress conditions.

articles.title: Diet at disease onset determines tissue inflammatory memory
articles.titleEn: Diet at disease onset determines tissue inflammatory memory
articles.abstract: Obesity, which is often associated with prolonged exposure to an obesogenic diet, substantially alters immunity 1–7 , but whether brief dietary changes shape acute inflammatory responses and long-term tissue memory remains unclear. Here we show that transient high-fat diet (HFD) exposure at the onset of acute type 17 skin inflammation exacerbates disease in lean mice to levels comparable to those associated with chronic obesity. This effect is restricted to a discrete 4-day peri-initiation window; HFD outside this window has no impact, whereas switching obese mice to a low-fat diet (LFD) during a similar window fully blunts disease amplification. Mechanistically, HFD rapidly recruits neutrophils into the skin, and neutrophils in challenged skin express high levels of Nlrp3 (ref. 8 ) and Il1b . Neutrophil depletion, genetic Nlrp3 deficiency and pharmacological NLRP3 inhibition each blunt the HFD-induced inflammatory amplification. These findings nominate a neutrophil–NLRP3–IL-1β axis that licences pathogenic IL-1R1 + CD4 + T helper type 17 (T H 17) cells 9,10 . After recovery, a chromatin-poised tissue-resident memory T cell population persists. Consequently, mice exposed to HFD at disease onset develop exaggerated inflammation upon recurrence, despite recovery and maintenance on LFD. Transient HFD similarly amplifies lung T H 17 inflammation through neutrophil- and IL-1R1-dependent mechanisms. Together, these findings show that dietary state during a narrow temporal window can durably reprogram disease trajectory, suggesting that short-lived physiological states may become embedded in local immune memory 11 when they coincide with tissue inflammation.

articles.title: Environmental RNA improves detection and surveillance of schistosomiasis transmission
articles.titleEn: Environmental RNA improves detection and surveillance of schistosomiasis transmission
articles.abstract: Environmental diagnosis of schistosomiasis, a disease affecting over 250 million people globally, remains challenging, thereby limiting efficient eradication efforts. Current methods, including environmental DNA (eDNA), cannot distinguish between infectious parasite life stages present in the environment. Here, we develop and validate an environmental RNA (eRNA) approach that enables detection and quantification of Schistosoma mansoni miracidia (infective to snails) and cercariae (infective to humans) directly from water samples. We identified life stage–specific transcripts and designed ddPCR assays highly specific to S. mansoni and each life stage. Laboratory experiments demonstrate that stage-specific eRNA assays accurately detect and quantify the relative abundance of each life stage. While eRNA and eDNA assays showed similar analytical limits of detection (LOD), eRNA provided enhanced organism-level detectability due to higher target molecule availability per life stage, also resulting in longer signal persistence in water that may facilitate the detection of the highly transient free-living stages of S. mansoni in the environment, especially cercariae. Field validation at six endemic sites in Brazil confirms that eRNA outperforms eDNA and conventional snail surveys in detecting S. mansoni cercariae indicating local transmission risk to humans. By enabling living stage discrimination and improving detectability compared to eDNA, our study advances both fundamental understanding and environmental surveillance of schistosomiasis transmission, supporting elimination initiatives in affected regions.

articles.title: A strain-insensitive multiplexed soft microneedle patch for robust interstitial fluid biomarker monitoring
articles.titleEn: A strain-insensitive multiplexed soft microneedle patch for robust interstitial fluid biomarker monitoring
articles.abstract: Wearable microneedle sensors analyze biomarkers in situ from interstitial fluids (ISF), enabling minimally invasive, precise, and continuous monitoring of metabolic diseases. However, conventional designs either lack adequate conformability to skin or suffer from electrode fractures during skin penetration and body motion, leading to signal instability that undermines reliable multiparameter acquisition. Here, we present a fully integrated system with a soft microneedle sensor array featuring nano-hill topographies on strain-resilient electrodes to delocalize strain via geometric confinement. This design reduces signal variability by 14-fold compared to conventional designs, enabling stable, simultaneous in situ monitoring of multiple ISF biomarkers. It achieves clinical-grade accuracy for continuous glucose monitoring (mean absolute relative difference of 10.8%) and captures dynamic synchronized variations in glucose, local tissue pH, and temperature in a living subject in real time. The system integrates a reusable electronic module with a disposable microneedle array with a sensor footprint of just 1.8 cm 2 . By combining high signal stability with multiparameter synchrony in a compact form factor, this system offers a practical solution for reliable, real-time ISF analysis under dynamic in vivo conditions.

articles.title: How Is Overland Flow Sediment Transport Capacity Affected by Biological Crusts?
articles.titleEn: How Is Overland Flow Sediment Transport Capacity Affected by Biological Crusts?
articles.abstract: Overland flow sediment transport capacity () governs soil detachment and sediment deposition processes, yet its regulation by biological soil crusts (BSCs), particularly across varying algae–moss community compositions, remains poorly quantified. In this study, five BSC community compositions spanning an algal‐ to moss‐dominated gradient were selected on the Loess Plateau. was measured using a scouring flume under six slope–discharge combinations (10°–25° and 0.2–1.0 L·s −1 ). The results showed that ranged from 0.99 to 12.30 kg·m −1 ·s −1 and was reduced by 11.47%–23.07% relative to bare soil, with progressively greater reductions from algae‐dominated to moss‐dominated crusts. Among the measured BSC characteristics, surface roughness showed the strongest negative correlation with and accounted for the largest unique fraction of its variation (59%) in the variation‐partitioning analysis of BSC characteristics. The relative contributions of BSC characteristics and hydraulic parameters varied with increasing hydraulic forcing, suggesting a transition toward greater hydraulic influence near a shear stress of 10 Pa. Two empirical power‐law equations incorporating surface roughness and shear stress provided good fits to the observed under the lower‐ and higher‐shear‐stress conditions, respectively. These findings demonstrate that BSC‐induced changes in surface roughness govern sediment transport under shallow overland flow conditions and provide a mechanistic framework for improving erosion prediction and ecological restoration in semi‐arid regions.

articles.title: Uncovering Responses of the Amazon Fluvial Lake System to the 2024 Drought by Fusing SWOT and Sentinel‐1 Observations
articles.titleEn: Uncovering Responses of the Amazon Fluvial Lake System to the 2024 Drought by Fusing SWOT and Sentinel‐1 Observations
articles.abstract: The 2024 Amazonian drought presented an unprecedented hydroclimatic anomaly. While prior research focused on atmospheric drivers and river impacts, the response of Amazon fluvial lake system (AFLs) has lacked large‐scale quantification. This study investigates the hydrological response of 838 fluvial lakes to the 2024 drought by integrating high‐resolution water surface elevation (WSE) data from the Surface Water and Ocean Topography (SWOT) mission with Sentinel‐1 water area observations. Lake‐specific dynamics were contextualized using basin‐wide terrestrial water storage anomalies (TWSA) from the GRACE‐FO mission. Results reveal that 95% of AFLs experienced persistent water level declines, averaging a −2.41 m anomaly relative to the 2018–2023 baseline. The response was spatially heterogeneous, with central sub‐basins exhibiting the most severe declines (average −3.53 m; maximum −13.82 m). Total AFLs storage loss peaked at ∼149 Gt during the 2024 drought, with 23% of the largest, most hydrologically‐connected lakes contributing over 86% of total deficit. The drought signal propagated systematically from west to east (upstream to downstream) over 75 days, confirmed by a strong positive correlation ( r = 0.67) between the timing of minimum WSE and lakes' longitudinal distance downstream. Furthermore, basin‐wide AFL storage changes correlated most strongly with TWSA at a 1‐month lag ( r = 0.94), although the lag corresponding to the strongest correlation varied among sub‐basins. Our findings provide the first basin‐scale, high‐resolution characterization of AFLs dynamics during an extreme drought by quantifying event's severity, spatial heterogeneity, and temporal propagation. These findings clarify how extreme droughts propagate through and deplete surface‐water storage across fluvial‐lake systems.

articles.title: OceanTracker 0.5: fast adaptable Lagrangian particle tracking in structured and unstructured grids
articles.titleEn: OceanTracker 0.5: fast adaptable Lagrangian particle tracking in structured and unstructured grids
articles.abstract: Particle tracking is frequently used to compute particle movements within hydrodynamic ocean models; however, modelling millions of particles is computationally challenging. OceanTracker is designed to reduce the time required to obtain results from particle tracking. Firstly, OceanTracker is computationally efficient, allowing users to simulate large numbers of particles in complex coastal environments, enabling improved statistics and exploration of a wider range of cases within acceptable run times. Secondly, OceanTracker can calculate multiple particle statistics during the computational run, eliminating the need to record and post-process large volumes of particle trajectories. The adaptability of OceanTracker's modular computational pipeline allows users to add and modify components that govern particle physics, behaviour, and statistics. The computational pipeline is entirely assembled from user-provided parameters, supplied as a JSON or YMAL text file or built using helper methods. Coders can easily modify existing components through code inheritance. Currently, OceanTracker supports hydrodynamic model output both for unstructured (SCHISM, FVCOM, DELFT3D-FM) and structured (ROMS, NEMO/GLORYS) grids. Computing the trajectories for more than one million particles with OceanTracker on a single computer core is more than ten times faster than the OpenDrift code and twice as fast as the Parcels code, despite treating structured grids as unstructured, which might be expected to be computationally slower than structured grids due to the time required to locate each particle within a hydrodynamic grid cell. In addition to its single-core performance, OceanTracker can run computations in parallel across available cores. This can further increase speed by up to an order of magnitude on currently available multicore desktop processors.

articles.title: Calibration guidelines and a runoff-isotope module for lake proxy system modeling (PRYSM v2.0)
articles.titleEn: Calibration guidelines and a runoff-isotope module for lake proxy system modeling (PRYSM v2.0)
articles.abstract: Lake sediments preserve information about past air temperature and precipitation, providing critical, real-world targets to validate climate models. However, these paleoclimate data encode information about multiple climate signals as well as lake dynamics, which makes comparison of paleoclimate data and model output challenging. Proxy system models (PSMs), or forward models that translate climate variables into proxy units, are tools for mechanistically interpreting paleoclimate data. PRYSM v2.0 is a PSM for paleoclimate data archived in lake sediments. Foundational to the accuracy of the PSM is a comprehensive understanding of the modern lake system supported by observations and meteorological inputs. However, two obstacles exist. First, stable oxygen and hydrogen isotope values in lake water are the target of many proxies preserved in lake sediments, but the PSM does not have a built-in catchment model to aid simulation of isotope values. Additionally, calibration of uncertain model parameters requires observations and expert knowledge of the lake system, yet most sites are unmonitored. Here, we advance PSMs for lake sediment archives by integrating a simple runoff-isotope module that can be adapted to any lake and reproduce the seasonal timing and magnitude of two mid-latitude lakes with contrasting morphometry, hydrology, and mixing regimes. Using multi-year observational datasets from the lakes, we conduct model experiments that require the PSM to predict the temperature and δ 2 H values of lake water when calibrated to a single observed profile, which mimics common observation collection challenges. For these lakes, observations from the warm, ice-free season are most informative and constrain uncertain parameter values that best generalize to unseen data from other water depths and years. Our framework for running and calibrating the PSM is available as open-source tools in Python, aiding the application of this PSM to the vast global database of lake sediment paleoclimate time series.

articles.title: GPU-accelerated three-dimensional variational data assimilation with automatic differentiation for WRF-Chem
articles.titleEn: GPU-accelerated three-dimensional variational data assimilation with automatic differentiation for WRF-Chem
articles.abstract: This study developed a PyTorch-based three-dimensional variational (3DVar) data assimilation system (PY3DVar) for the Weather Research and Forecasting model coupled to Chemistry (WRF-Chem), which integrates automatic differentiation (AD) to replace traditional manual gradient derivation and adopts Graphics Processing Unit (GPU) acceleration for high computational efficiency. PY3DVar enables the simultaneous assimilation of gaseous pollutants (SO 2 , NO 2 , CO, O 3 ) and particulate matter (PM 2.5 , PM 10 ) and supports flexible deployment on both Central Processing Unit (CPU) and GPU computing platforms. Idealized tests were first conducted to verify the physical consistency of the assimilation system. Twenty consecutive real-case assimilation experiments, each followed by a 24 h forecast, were then conducted to assess computational performance and efficiency, benchmarked against the classic Fortran-based 3DVar system (FT3DVar) using CPU parallelization. The results of the idealized tests show PY3DVar effectively propagates observation information, generating increment fields consistent with FT3DVar. Long-term real-case experiments further verify that the two assimilation systems achieve nearly identical analysis accuracy for chemical initial fields. On the GPU platform, PY3DVar achieves an average assimilation time of 1.2 s, representing a 26.2-fold speedup compared to FT3DVar on 64 CPU cores (32.7 s). Parallel scalability tests across 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 and 64 CPU cores reveal that FT3DVar runs faster per iteration across all core counts. Consequently, FT3DVar achieves shorter total assimilation time on 1, 2, 4 and 16 cores, whereas PY3DVar outperforms it at 8, 32 and 64 cores, owing to its intrinsically fewer required iterations for convergence. The average 24 h forecast results show that the improved initial fields have sustained positive effects on short-term forecasts: the improvements persist for over 24 h for SO 2 , CO, PM 2.5 , and PM 10 , and for over 6 h for NO 2 and O 3 . These results demonstrate that PY3DVar delivers substantially faster assimilation than FT3DVar while maintaining equivalent analysis accuracy, offering an efficient and practical solution for operational atmospheric chemical data assimilation.

articles.title: On combining climate models into weighted ensembles
articles.titleEn: On combining climate models into weighted ensembles
articles.abstract: Several methods have been proposed and used to refine estimates of future climate change based on combined output from comprehensive climate models. While previously the so-called model democracy approach was used to combine model outputs, where every model is given equal weight, it is now widely accepted that using model weights that account for model performance and model independence is necessary to obtain more reliable results. However, most existing approaches rely, implicitly or explicitly, on a similar statistical basis, while describing things in different ways. Here we distinguish between approaches that are based on the performance of individual models (individual performance weighting) and approaches that are based on the performance of the weighted ensemble as a whole (ensemble performance weighting). At the same time, we formulate both in probabilistic Bayesian terms to make their application and comparison straightforward. Using simple constructed examples, we demonstrate that the ensemble performance weighting approach implicitly accounts for co-dependencies among models, which arguably makes the computation of independence weights for the purpose of model weighting obsolete. We also show that a set of weighted models within the ensemble weighting approach will naturally tend to artificially reduce uncertainty and that this is strongly influenced by the choice of the prior distribution over weight vectors. The distinction between individual and ensemble performance weighting is both methodological and conceptual. Formulating both approaches in general probabilistic Bayesian terms as done here, can serve as a common basis for future developments with regard to ensemble model weighting in Earth system science. The discussed concepts are generally applicable across domains and are thus possibly relevant for other modeling communities as well.

articles.title: DETECT: seismological data from multiple dense arrays deployed across the Irpinia fault system in southern Italy
articles.titleEn: DETECT: seismological data from multiple dense arrays deployed across the Irpinia fault system in southern Italy
articles.abstract: We present a large seismological dataset (https://geofon.gfz.de/doi/network/ZK/2021, last access: 14 October 2026) composed of continuous recordings from 200 temporary stations (seismic network ZK, https://doi.org/10.14470/MX7576871994, Bindi et al., 2021), which operated continuously for approximately one year in the Southern Apennines (Southern Italy) as part of the DETECT experiment. The dataset is compliant with the seismological standards for the archiving of data and metadata, and with standardized tools for disseminating them, e.g., the International Federation of Digital Seismograph Networks (FDSN) web services. The data set was collected during the DETECT experiment in the Irpinia area (southern Italy), which is one of the regions with the highest seismic hazard in Italy. In this contribution, we provide details on how to download waveform data and station metadata, as well as information on data availability and quality.

articles.title: BorFIT: a novel LiDAR-based training dataset for individual tree segmentation and species detection in northern boreal forests
articles.titleEn: BorFIT: a novel LiDAR-based training dataset for individual tree segmentation and species detection in northern boreal forests
articles.abstract: BorFIT is a novel northern boreal forest training dataset designed to assist in the segmentation of individual trees and the detection of species from uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV)-LiDAR point clouds, thus contributing to deep learning-based forestry applications. Recent advancements in AI-supported individual tree detection have shown significant progress; however, satisfactory results remain elusive in dense and structurally-complex boreal forests. We compiled a training dataset designed to remedy this issue. BorFIT comprises 384 UAV-LiDAR point clouds, each with an area of 20 m × 20 m, in the form of reference plots, with up to 200 manually segmented and species classified trees per point cloud. The BorFIT training dataset is derived from UAV-LiDAR surveys at 146 sites carried out between 2021 and 2024 in East Siberia (Yakutia), northwest Canada, and Alaska (USA). The sites were selected along bioclimatic gradients to represent the circumboreal region. From each UAV-LiDAR transect derived point cloud, we extracted a minimum of four reference plots (each 20 m × 20 m) based on maximum tree heights within the plots to systematically sample the apparent tree density gradient. We manually segmented identifiable trees within each reference plot point cloud leading to 16 530 individual trees in total. Following individual tree segmentation, we trained four random forest classifiers for different regions to predict the species of every segmented tree. The predicted tree species include: Picea mariana Britton, Sterns & Poggenb., Picea sitchensis Bong. Carrière, Picea glauca Moench, Voss, Pinus contorta Douglas ex Loudon, Abies lasiocarpa Hook., Nutt., Larix laricina Du Roi, K. Koch, Betula papyrifera Marshall, Betula neoalaskana Regel, Ashburner McAll., Populus balsamifera L., Populus tremuloides Michx., Pinus sylvestris Thunb. and Alnus spp. The data offer the means for 3D space analysis of species distribution and stand structure around the circumboreal region. Furthermore, it can be used as a training dataset for artificial intelligence (AI) applications, and thereby improve our understanding of the boreal forest's vegetation reorganization in response to significant global warming (https://doi.org/10.1594/PANGAEA.980505, Kruse et al., 2026).

articles.title: Optimal Biomass Allocation to Leaves Across Global Terrestrial Ecosystems
articles.titleEn: Optimal Biomass Allocation to Leaves Across Global Terrestrial Ecosystems
articles.abstract: Leaves influence global climate and water resources by regulating the flows of CO 2 , energy and water between the atmosphere and land. Here we developed a theoretical framework that predicts the optimal annual fraction of biomass production allocated to the production of new leaves ( η f ) as the product of the optimal leaf area index (LAI) and the optimal ratio of leaf mass–per–area to the leaf life cycle (LMA/LC), divided by annual total biomass production (BP). All quantities depend on local environmental variables, with different solutions (embedding a climatic aridity effect on optimal LMA/LC) for evergreen and deciduous plants. Using a global compilation of η f data, we show that this theory predicts the emergent responses of η f to growing–season temperature and aridity. These responses arise from the trade‐offs among the environmental sensitivities of LMA/LC, LAI and BP. It is predicted that the rising CO 2 is steadily reducing the fraction of biomass production allocated to leaves.

articles.title: Divergent Spatial Climate Associations of the Microbial Nitrogen Pump Across a Subtropical Cropland‐Forest Transect
articles.titleEn: Divergent Spatial Climate Associations of the Microbial Nitrogen Pump Across a Subtropical Cropland‐Forest Transect
articles.abstract: Soil microbial necromass nitrogen (MNN) represents a persistent organic N pool, yet how land use modulates its spatial content and biomass‐normalized ratio across climatic gradients remains elusive. Across paired forest and cropland soils spanning a subtropical climatic gradient in southwestern China, we quantified fungal, bacterial, and total MNN contents using amino sugar biomarkers. Microbial N growth and gross N mineralization were measured using 18 O‐H 2 O tracing and 15 N pool dilution, respectively, and were combined to estimate microbial N use efficiency (NUE). We then compared MNN content and its accumulation coefficient between land uses and examined their associations with mean annual temperature (MAT), mean annual precipitation (MAP), and microbial NUE. Forest soils contained 341.4% more fungal necromass N and 150.6% more total MNN than croplands, but had a lower microbial necromass N accumulation coefficient (MNNAC), defined as the ratio of MNN to microbial biomass N (MBN). In forests, fungal and total microbial necromass N contents, as well as fungal and total microbial necromass N accumulation coefficients, were negatively associated with both MAT and MAP, whereas corresponding climatic associations were weak or absent in croplands. Microbial NUE was positively associated with MNN content in forest soils but negatively associated with MNN content in croplands. In contrast, a significant negative association between NUE and MNNAC was observed only in cropland soils. Multivariate analyses identified distinct correlates of MNN: weathering, plant biomass, resource availability, and soil organic matter evenness in forests, but clay‐mediated mineral protection and resource stoichiometric imbalance in croplands. These findings indicate that land use redefines the spatial climate associations of the microbial N pump, suggesting context dependence within the Microbial Efficiency–Matrix Stabilization (MEMS) framework and supporting the inclusion of land‐use context in Earth system models of terrestrial nitrogen feedbacks under global change.

articles.title: Liquid polymer enhances methanogenesis and restructures prokaryotic communities in freshwater sediments
articles.titleEn: Liquid polymer enhances methanogenesis and restructures prokaryotic communities in freshwater sediments
articles.abstract: The widespread use of synthetic hydrophilic polymers, such as polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP), has raised concerns about their potential effects on environmental biogeochemical processes, yet their impact on sediment ecosystems remains largely unexplored. We investigated how PVP influences methane (CH 4 ) production and prokaryotic community composition in freshwater sediments over a 56 d anoxic incubation. PVP exposure accelerated the onset of methanogenesis, increased maximum CH 4 production rates, and elevated maximum CH 4 concentrations. Notably, a substantial proportion of the response occurred already at environmentally relevant concentrations. These functional changes were accompanied by shifts in bacterial communities, particularly among fermentative taxa known to produce key methanogenic substrates. In contrast, archaeal communities, including methanogens, exhibited comparatively weak and transient responses. The concomitant increase in CO 2 and CH 4 production and the observed microbial community shifts suggest that PVP altered microbial carbon-processing pathways, although the mechanisms responsible for these effects remain unresolved. As a proof-of-concept study, our results provide initial evidence that a widespread synthetic hydrophilic polymer can modify sediment microbial communities and stimulate methane production. These findings highlight the need for future studies addressing the mechanistic basis of these responses and their relevance under environmentally realistic conditions.

articles.title: Synthesis of greenhouse gas emission factors for forest organic soils in the Köppen–Geiger Dfb climate zone
articles.titleEn: Synthesis of greenhouse gas emission factors for forest organic soils in the Köppen–Geiger Dfb climate zone
articles.abstract: Greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from organic soils are a key component of land-use-related emissions, particularly in countries with large areas of organic soils. Temperate-zone forest soils remain less studied in GHG research than boreal soils. However, recent work has expanded coverage in the northeastern temperate region, which, under the Köppen–Geiger climate classification, shares key climatic characteristics with the southern boreal region (Dfb). This study synthesised updated GHG flux data to evaluate carbon balance and emissions from forest organic soils in the Dfb zone, stratified by drainage status, nutrient availability, and dominant tree species. Such stratification revealed CO 2 source-sink patterns, which encourage the ecological relevance of using these categories for data aggregation. The dominant tree species reflected nutrient status: drained coniferous and deciduous stands have been reported as CO 2 sources, emitting 0.03 ± 0.55 and 0.47 ± 0.29 t CO 2 -C ha −1 yr −1 , respectively, though soils tended to shift toward CO 2 sinks in stands older than 25 years. In contrast, undrained soils have generally been observed to function as CO 2 sinks, although not necessarily in all sites. However, this stratification was less informative for CH 4 and N 2 O. CH 4 fluxes were primarily determined by water table level rather than by other site variables, whereas N 2 O showed a tendency toward elevated emissions in deciduous stands, irrespective of drainage status.

articles.title: Mobility of dry granular flows over contrasting erodible bed materials in laboratory experiments
articles.titleEn: Mobility of dry granular flows over contrasting erodible bed materials in laboratory experiments
articles.journal: Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences
articles.abstract: Erosion and entrainment exchange mass and momentum across the flow–bed interface and can strongly modify mass-flow mobility. However, the material properties that control whether erosive flows accelerate, decelerate, or maintain their mobility remain insufficiently understood. Here, we conducted dry granular flow experiments to investigate erosion, flow evolution, and deposition across systematically imposed flow–bed contrasts, using surface measurements of the evolving flow and final deposit. A quartz slide of constant solid particle density was released over beds with lower, equal, and higher solid particle densities and compared with a reference case without erosion. Each scenario was repeated using finer sand-sized particles and coarser sand-to-gravel-sized particles. The low-density beds produced deeper erosion, higher average flow-front velocities, and longer runout. By contrast, the equal- and high-density beds produced nearly identical results, with shallower erosion depths, lower average flow-front velocities, and more compact deposits, despite their substantially different solid particle densities. The same relative patterns were observed for both particle-size fractions, although coarse-particle flows generally formed longer and flatter deposits. This asymmetric response shows that mobility cannot be explained by solid particle density alone. Instead, the enhanced mobility over the low-density beds is more consistently explained by coupled effects of lower internal friction, rounded particle shape, greater bed deformation, and more efficient entrainment. The similar response of the equal- and high-density beds reflects their comparable and higher frictional resistance and angular particle shape, which appear to outweigh the contrast in solid particle density under the tested conditions. Yet, surface-based measurements alone cannot resolve whether more subtle differences persist in basal slip, shear localization, and the incorporation of mobilized bed material. Depth-resolved observations at the flow–bed interface are therefore needed to directly relate erosion and entrainment to mass and momentum exchange.

articles.title: Large-scale flood monitoring based on time-series Sentinel-1 images and Z -score
articles.titleEn: Large-scale flood monitoring based on time-series Sentinel-1 images and Z -score
articles.journal: Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences
articles.abstract: Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) satellites have emerged as a crucial technology for real-time flood monitoring in the face of escalating flood disaster hazards. However, existing flood extraction techniques still face challenges in simultaneously achieving accurate urban inundation detection and extensive large-scale monitoring. To address this challenge, this study proposes a time-series Sentinel-1 SAR anomaly-detection approach based on an analysis of backscatter characteristics across different land-cover types and the integration of auxiliary datasets. First, an analysis of scattering behaviour in time-series SAR images revealed that, in natural areas, the consistency of backscatter intensity is strongly influenced by vegetation growth status. In building areas, rainfall and floodwater can intensify or suppress double-bounce scattering depending on building geometry and water depth, thereby disrupting intensity consistency. Based on these findings, a Z -score-based flood classification tree was developed. The method uses reference images and flood-period images to compute standardized anomaly maps with statistical interpretability under approximate normality and establishes operationally transparent flood-detection thresholds. The integration of VV and VH polarizations within the classification tree further improves the reliability of flood identification. Applied to the 2021 Weihui flood event, the method demonstrated strong performance, achieving a critical success index (CSI) of 60 % and overall accuracy (OA) of 90 % in natural areas, and a CSI of 62 % and OA of 73 % in building areas. The proposed approach shows significant advantages in accurately classifying flood-affected areas and offers the capability to monitor both large-scale floods and urban inundation.

articles.title: Evolutionary oxidation of proteins in Earth’s history
articles.titleEn: Evolutionary oxidation of proteins in Earth’s history
articles.abstract: Evidence for Earth’s oxygenation during the Great Oxidation Event (GOE) and Neoproterozoic Oxidation Event (NOE) comes primarily from the geological record. We report rising oxidation state of carbon (Zc) in proteins over billion-year timescales, a consistent trend recovered from diverse genomic datasets. Combining statistical and thermodynamic modeling, we link this trend to environmental drivers including Earth’s progressive oxygenation and secular cooling. The oxidation trend appears in the amino acid composition of modern genomes from methanogens and sulfur-cycling organisms, phylostratigraphic gene age groups in eukaryotes, and reconstructed ancestral sequences for Rubisco, nitrogenase, thioredoxin, and 3-isopropylmalate dehydrogenase (IPMDH). Major Zc steps broadly overlap the GOE but do not exactly coincide with it; uncertainties in phylogenetic age and limited spatial associations complicate direct comparison with geochemical proxies. Gene age groups in unicellular, but not multicellular, eukaryotes show a second rise of protein Zc around the NOE. These widespread genomic signatures of protein oxidation are consistent with a thermodynamic hypothesis in which energy minimization directs protein sequence evolution across metabolic functions.

articles.title: CPRISP: an interpretable deep learning framework predicting circRNA-RBP interactions and guiding therapeutic discovery in neurodegeneration
articles.titleEn: CPRISP: an interpretable deep learning framework predicting circRNA-RBP interactions and guiding therapeutic discovery in neurodegeneration
articles.abstract: Circular RNAs regulate gene expression through interactions with ribonucleic acid binding proteins, but their binding sites remain difficult to predict across proteins and cellular contexts. Existing methods often focus on transcript features while making limited use of protein-specific information and structural context. Here, we show that an integrated deep learning framework combining circular transcript sequence composition, physicochemical properties, secondary structure, pretrained representations and protein features improves interaction-site prediction across 37 benchmark datasets and generalizes across cell lines; model interpretation recovers conserved single-stranded sequence patterns, while analyses of proteins linked to Alzheimer disease, Parkinson disease and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis identify recurrent pathways involving nucleocytoplasmic transport, lysosomal signaling and guanosine triphosphatase activity and prioritize compounds for experimental follow-up, supporting accurate and interpretable mapping of circular ribonucleic acid protein interactions without implying therapeutic efficacy.

articles.title: Carbonation of silicate minerals contributes to atmospheric CO2 drawdown in glacier-fed streams
articles.titleEn: Carbonation of silicate minerals contributes to atmospheric CO2 drawdown in glacier-fed streams
articles.abstract: Glaciers produce abundant grains of reactive minerals that influence inorganic carbon cycling, yet the links between mineral weathering and CO 2 dynamics in glacier-fed streams (GFSs) remain poorly understood. Here we combine streamwater geochemistry, solute end-member modelling, carbonate saturation calculations and suspended-sediment mineralogy across 170 GFSs worldwide. We show that 69% of GFSs were undersaturated with respect to atmospheric CO 2 equilibrium, indicating widespread atmospheric CO 2 uptake. Grain-scale analyses of selected carbonate-bearing GFSs reveal metastable Mg-bearing carbonate phases consistent with secondary mineral formation in transient microenvironments. We propose that CO 2 released during sulfuric acid-driven carbonate weathering and secondary calcite precipitation can be partly consumed by carbonation of silicate- and clay-derived mineral surfaces, transferring dissolved inorganic carbon into particulate inorganic carbon. This sediment-mediated pathway can contribute to CO 2 undersaturation under favourable lithological and geochemical conditions, revealing a previously underappreciated coupling between chemical weathering, sediment–water interactions and inorganic carbon storage in proglacial landscapes rapidly expanding under global glacier retreat.

articles.title: Satellite‐Based Assessment Reveals Patterns of Coastal Marsh Carbon Sequestration Along the U.S. East and Gulf Coasts
articles.titleEn: Satellite‐Based Assessment Reveals Patterns of Coastal Marsh Carbon Sequestration Along the U.S. East and Gulf Coasts
articles.abstract: Coastal marshes are critical blue‐carbon ecosystems, yet regional quantification of vegetation‐derived carbon burial and living biomass carbon stocks within marshes remains limited. Here, we developed a transparent, measurement‐based framework integrating Sentinel‐2 data (2019–2024), field biomass measurements, marsh‐type distribution maps, and literature‐derived marsh‐type‐specific carbon allocation parameters to estimate living biomass carbon stocks and vegetation‐derived burial rates across tidal marshes of the U.S. East and Gulf Coasts. Among tested vegetation indices (VIs), the Green Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (GNDVI) showed the strongest relationship with field‐measured above‐ground biomass (AGB) across seasons and marsh types. Applying the calibrated GNDVI–AGB relationship, we mapped annual peak AGB and used seasonal AGB differences as a satellite proxy for net above‐ground primary production (NAPP). articles.title: Spatiotemporal Propagation and Future Risks of Agricultural Drought in Response to Meteorological Drought Across Asia
articles.titleEn: Spatiotemporal Propagation and Future Risks of Agricultural Drought in Response to Meteorological Drought Across Asia
articles.abstract: Under the background of global warming, drought risk has intensified. Clarifying the changing patterns and response relationships of different drought types is vital for risk management and climate change adaptation. Using multi‐model data from the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase VI (CMIP6) and an improved three‐dimensional clustering algorithm, this study identified meteorological and Agricultural drought (AD) events in Asia. We analyzed the spatiotemporal differentiation, migration patterns, and response relationships between the two drought types under different future Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs). The results showed that, under the historical scenario, AD events outnumbered Meteorological drought (MD) events by 77 occurrences, while their average duration was 0.2 months shorter than that of meteorological droughts. The spatiotemporal correlation between meteorological and AD varied regionally, being strongest in Central Asia and southern East Asia, while weak or negative in North Asia and the Qinghai‐Tibet Plateau. Under future scenarios, from SSP1‐2.6 to SSP5‐8.5 scenario, meteorological droughts exhibited longer duration, and both types showed higher severity. The average duration of MD events increased from 2.3 to 3.9 months, and the average migration distance extended from 1,166.3 km to 2,650.4 km. The proportion of matched pairs in which MD preceded AD rose from 29% under SSP1‐2.6% to 60% under SSP5‐8.5. Under the scenarios of SSP2‐4.5, SSP3‐7.0 and SSP5‐8.5, a model‐derived crossover between the fitted SPEI and SSMI trends occurs around 2058. These findings reveal the complex and transitive nature of future drought risk in Asia and provide a scientific basis for formulating targeted drought‐resistance strategies.

articles.title: Imminent Emergence of Permanent Surface Marine Heatwave States Across Global Oceans
articles.titleEn: Imminent Emergence of Permanent Surface Marine Heatwave States Across Global Oceans
articles.abstract: Marine heatwaves (MHWs) can devastate ocean ecosystems, yet the timing at which anthropogenic changes in MHW characteristics permanently emerge from natural variability at the global scale remains poorly quantified. Here, we present the first global time of emergence analysis of MHW characteristics of the ocean surface using simulations from 21 Earth system models from the sixth Coupled Model Intercomparison Project under moderate (SSP2‐4.5) and high (SSP5‐8.5) greenhouse gas emissions scenarios. Relative to a 1985–2014 baseline, we find that almost 48% of the global ocean has already experienced significant trends in both annual MHW days and frequency. Across tropical oceans, MHW conditions permanently emerge between 2020 and 2040 regardless of emission pathway, indicating that near‐term transformation is unavoidable. By mid‐century, half the global ocean is projected to experience MHW conditions for at least 50% of the year, increasing to 90% by 2100. Regions experiencing the strongest warming show the earliest emergence, with uncertainty in emergence timing comparatively low in the tropics (10–15 years) but expanding substantially at higher latitudes (30 years). These findings demonstrate that persistent, large‐scale marine thermal stress is imminent, demanding transformation from reactive crisis management to anticipatory ocean governance within the next two decades.

articles.title: Climate‐Driven Straightening of Western North Pacific Tropical Cyclone Trajectories
articles.titleEn: Climate‐Driven Straightening of Western North Pacific Tropical Cyclone Trajectories
articles.abstract: Tropical cyclone (TC) trajectory shifts remain a critical uncertainty in climate risk assessment. However, due to the absence of effective quantification methods for TC trajectories, our understanding of the overall characteristics of their trajectory shifts and the underlying impact mechanisms remains quite limited. Here, we introduce an important metric, sinuosity, as the parameter to describe the overall trajectory of TCs, and propose a new sinuosity‐based machine learning framework for their classification. The findings reveal a significant decrease in the sinuosity of TC trajectories over the Western North Pacific. This reduction is mainly due to straighter trajectories within the recurving cluster TCs, which follow conventional southeast‐to‐northeast recurving trajectories, with most dissipating in Northeast Asia. This “straightening” phenomenon of recurving TCs is jointly driven by the shortening of TC duration and the westward expansion of the Western Pacific Subtropical High (WPSH). As the trajectories of recurving TCs are becoming straighter, they are more likely to make landfall in Northeast Asia, significantly increasing the regional risks of TCs. These findings unravel a previously unobserved dimension of TC climate response, demonstrating how changes in subtropical circulations are reshaping regional hazard patterns with profound implications for disaster preparedness, mitigation, and adaptation strategies.

articles.title: Synergistic Management of Abandoned Cropland Mitigates Trade‐Offs Between Food Security and Climate Mitigation in Hilly and Mountainous Areas
articles.titleEn: Synergistic Management of Abandoned Cropland Mitigates Trade‐Offs Between Food Security and Climate Mitigation in Hilly and Mountainous Areas
articles.abstract: Abandoned cropland is a crucial strategic reserve to reconcile food security (SDG 2) and climate mitigation (SDG 13). However, maximizing these co‐benefits in ecologically fragile hilly regions is constrained by intense spatial competition between food and carbon. In this study, we proposed a spatial decision‐making framework that integrates suitability assessment and Pareto optimization to quantify trade‐offs and identify synergistic pathways in a typical hilly province of Southwest China. The results showed that although the remaining abandoned cropland had substantial potential for either food (4.0 × 10 11 kcal yr −1 ) or carbon (1.38 × 10 6 t CO 2 yr −1 ), the dual‐suitability overlap rate reached 69.1%, leading to high opportunity costs under single‐objective management. Crucially, scenario simulations and Pareto analysis identified Pareto‐efficient compromise solutions for balancing regional benefits. When spatial prioritization was combined with intensified management, food and carbon potentials could be increased by 125.0% and 51.6%, respectively, without expanding beyond abandoned cropland. These findings highlight that governing abandoned cropland in complex terrain requires spatially differentiated zoning that distinguishes food‐dominant, carbon‐dominant, and synergistic management zones to achieve regional synergistic gains.

articles.title: Braided Rivers as Morphological States: A Data‐Driven Identification of Recurrent Planform Configurations
articles.titleEn: Braided Rivers as Morphological States: A Data‐Driven Identification of Recurrent Planform Configurations
articles.abstract: Braided rivers reorganize their channels from time to time, featuring complex morphological dynamics and intermittent sediment transport that are difficult to describe using scalar metrics or single representative configurations. To better capture this complexity, we introduce a stochastic approach, which involves tracking the planform dynamics of channels and the associated bedload transport rates. In this approach, each state represents a given planform channel geometry, and the system can randomly transition from one state to another over time. We conducted a 1‐month laboratory experiment. We identified morphological states from plan view images using an automated workflow combining several techniques (image comparison metrics, dimensionality reduction, and density clustering). The sequence of states revealed long periods of morphological stability, separated by short periods of channel reorganization. Bed morphology also showed great diversity, ranging from narrow, single‐thread channels to large, braiding networks prone to sediment storage. While earlier studies have revealed the chaotic nature of modeled braided system evolution, which implies the unpredictability of exact configurations, we found that: (a) there was a limited number of recurrent states; (b) the lifetime of each morphological state was associated with a well‐defined timescale; (c) there were preferential transitions from one state to another; and (d) bed morphological states were related to the variability of the sediment transport rate.

articles.title: Technical note: Machine learning metamodelling for global sensitivity analysis
articles.titleEn: Technical note: Machine learning metamodelling for global sensitivity analysis
articles.abstract: Global sensitivity analysis (GSA) plays a central role in hydrologic modelling by supporting model understanding, diagnosis, and decision-making through the identification of influential and non-influential parameters and their interactions. Variance-based methods provide a rigorous framework for GSA but are often computationally expensive, as their estimation requires a large number of model evaluations. Metamodelling has therefore been widely adopted as a strategy to alleviate this issue, with recent advances in machine learning (ML) offering new opportunities to construct accurate and flexible surrogates for complex models. This technical note examines the practical relationship between Sobol' total-effect indices ( T i ) and feature importance measures derived from ML metamodels within a hydrologic modelling context. Building on theoretical results that link T i to permutation variable importance (PVI i ) under independence assumptions, we provide systematic numerical evidence using three hydrologic models of varying complexity (HBV, HyMod, and VIC) applied to three headwater catchments in northern Germany, together with three ML metamodels: a gradient boosting decision tree (GBDT), a neural network (NN), and a linear model (LM). The three metamodels were trained on Monte Carlo samples and used to estimate sensitivities through PVI i and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP i ). The results demonstrate that GBDT and NN metamodels reliably reproduce both the ranking and relative magnitude of T i using PVI i across all hydrologic models, providing clear empirical support for the theoretical connection between the two measures. In contrast, the performance of LM-based estimates depends strongly on the degree of linearity in the underlying model response. Mean absolute SHAP i values exhibit a consistent monotonic relationship with T i and preserve parameter rankings, while sample-specific SHAP i values enable a distributed evaluation of sensitivities across both the parameter space and the target variable space. Overall, this study highlights ML metamodelling as a computationally efficient and conceptually sound framework for GSA in hydrologic modelling and beyond.

articles.title: Non-stationary low-flow frequency analysis with mixed Weibull components and Copula-based dependence framework
articles.titleEn: Non-stationary low-flow frequency analysis with mixed Weibull components and Copula-based dependence framework
articles.abstract: Extreme low flows are a pressing challenge for water management, reducing water availability and degrading water quality. Reliable design estimates are therefore essential. Traditional low-flow frequency analysis relies on the assumption of independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) data, which is increasingly violated under climate change and by varying low-flow generating processes. In a seasonal snow-influenced climate, annual low-flow extremes may occur in both summer and winter, potentially exhibiting seasonal dependence that challenges conventional modelling approaches. This study extends traditional low-flow frequency analysis to non-stationary conditions by jointly accounting for temporal trends, seasonal heterogeneity and inter-event dependence. Building on previously developed mixed distribution and mixed copula frameworks, we generalise these frameworks to non-stationary conditions using three-parameter Weibull distributions. Seasonal low-flow distributions and their joint mixture vary over time, with linear non-stationarity in the location parameter and in inter-event dependence. Results are presented for more than 700 catchments from the European Reference Observatory of Basins for INternational hydrological climate change detection (ROBIN) dataset. Model evaluation shows that neglecting non-stationarity when present can lead to biased assessments of low-flow severity, particularly for higher return periods. In contrast, non-stationary models provide a more realistic representation of evolving low-flow regimes by revealing temporal changes that remain hidden from traditional estimators. By preserving the conceptual consistency of the previous stationary framework, the proposed non-stationary framework improves the statistical characterisation of extreme low flows and provides an enhanced basis for low-flow frequency analysis by offering new insights into past and current low-flow processes under climate change.

articles.title: Including the triple isotopic composition of dissolved oxygen in the ocean into the iLOVECLIM model (version 1.1.7): development and evaluation
articles.titleEn: Including the triple isotopic composition of dissolved oxygen in the ocean into the iLOVECLIM model (version 1.1.7): development and evaluation
articles.abstract: Contributing around half of the oxygen produced on Earth, marine photosynthetic production is one of the main mechanisms for carbon fixation, with a central role in the oxygen cycle. The triple isotopic composition of atmospheric oxygen ( 17 Δ), measured in ice cores, provides a global integrator of past biospheric oxygen fluxes, which can also provide indirect constraints on associated carbon-cycle processes. However, deconvolving the signal of 17 Δ requires one to isolate the contribution of oceanic biosphere productivity ( 17 Δ ocean ) from those of the terrestrial biosphere ( 17 Δ terr ) and the stratosphere ( 17 Δ strato ). Here, we present the first implementation of 17 Δ ocean in the intermediate-complexity climate model iLOVECLIM. The three main processes controlling 17 Δ ocean , i.e. photosynthesis, respiration, and air–sea gas exchange, are explicitly represented and evaluated under preindustrial conditions. Model results show overall good agreement with available measurements, particularly in the Pacific Ocean. In contrast, systematic overestimation is found in the Southern Ocean. At fixed stations, seasonality is reproduced but with underestimated amplitude. These discrepancies mainly reflect challenges in representing remineralization and oxygen minimum zones, and highlight opportunities to refine the representation of primary productivity and vertical mixing. Overall, this new implementation provides the first coupled model framework for simulating 17 Δ ocean , both as a diagnostic of biogeochemical processes and as a tool for reconstructing past changes in marine productivity. Extending the implementation to the terrestrial biosphere will further allow reconstruction of the past global biosphere and direct comparison with 17 Δ records from ice cores.

articles.title: Stochastic homogeneous freezing of supercooled droplets in mixed-phase clouds in particle-based idealised microphysics framework (exemplified with PySDM v3.0)
articles.titleEn: Stochastic homogeneous freezing of supercooled droplets in mixed-phase clouds in particle-based idealised microphysics framework (exemplified with PySDM v3.0)
articles.abstract: Homogeneous freezing of supercooled cloud droplets is an important process governing ice formation during the transition from mixed-phase clouds to pure ice-phase clouds in the upper troposphere. In this study, we implement a stochastic representation of homogeneous freezing in the particle-based aerosol–cloud microphysics model PySDM, treating freezing as a Poisson process dependent on droplet volume, time step, and the nucleation rate. We compare two parameterisations of the nucleation rate: a temperature-dependent formulation and a saturation-dependent formulation. Using an idealised adiabatically ascending air-parcel framework, we investigate the distribution of freezing temperatures and the resulting ice number concentrations across ensembles that vary updraft speed, cloud condensation nuclei number concentration, droplet size distribution, and the number of super-particles. Simulations are performed both with and without vapour deposition on ice, enabling assessment of the role of the Wegener-Bergeron-Findeisen process. We find that homogeneous freezing occurs over a broad temperature range rather than at a single threshold, with freezing temperatures strongly controlled by cooling rate and droplet size. When vapour deposition on ice is active, early stochastic freezing events dominate the evolution of the frozen droplet fraction and substantially reduce the fraction of droplets that ultimately freeze. The two nucleation-rate formulations produce similar behaviour near water saturation but diverge significantly when supersaturation or subsaturation with respect to water develops, leading to pronounced differences in freezing temperatures and ice number concentrations. Our results highlight the importance of stochastic freezing formulations and nucleation-rate choice for representing cloud glaciation in models.

articles.title: Five Decades of Citizen Science Reveal Erosion of Hotspots of Multifaceted Plant Diversity
articles.titleEn: Five Decades of Citizen Science Reveal Erosion of Hotspots of Multifaceted Plant Diversity
articles.abstract: Biodiversity includes taxonomic, phylogenetic, and functional diversity but the changes in these facets at regional scales remain unclear and often context dependent. Using 2.5 million citizen science observations of 1957 vascular plant species across 53 years in SW‐Germany, we assessed changes in seven biodiversity metrics. Rather than a general decline, we found different facets exhibited different trends in both direction and magnitude of change. Phylogenetic and taxonomic diversity change were mostly negatively correlated, and change in functional diversity was independent from the others. We identified the role of climate and human activity influencing the change in taxonomic and functional diversity, while phylogenetic diversity was also affected by geodiversity. Crucially, we detected consistent erosion of biodiversity hotspots across all facets, while areas with low initial diversity tended to gain species. These findings highlight the need to consider multiple biodiversity facets and local context dependency to better understand biodiversity change at regional scales.

articles.title: Dependence of seismic hazard assessment on the observation time interval: insights from a synthetic earthquake catalogue in southeastern Spain
articles.titleEn: Dependence of seismic hazard assessment on the observation time interval: insights from a synthetic earthquake catalogue in southeastern Spain
articles.journal: Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences
articles.abstract: Traditionally Probabilistic Seismic Hazard Assessment (PSHA) is mainly based on historical and instrumental catalogues. The seismic catalogue in SE Spain covers a period of almost 1 kyr. Although this catalogue can be considered long, its time span is not enough to record the complete seismic cycle of the slow moving regional faults, for example, the ones which conform the Eastern Betics Shear Zone (EBSZ). To assess whether the seismic hazard at the EBSZ depends on the time interval in which the earthquake catalogue has been recorded, this study performs a PSHA using synthetic seismicity. The synthetic seismicity in the EBSZ consists of a 1 Myr catalogue generated in previous studies using the RSQSim earthquake simulator, applied to the fault system that forms the EBSZ. This catalogue has been divided into ten thousand sub-catalogues of the same duration as the historical and instrumental one and randomly distributed over time. The magnitude-frequency distributions of the synthetic sub-catalogues show significant variability in the maximum reached magnitude, in the slope of the Gutenberg-Richter relationship and in the annual rate of earthquakes. A hundred sub-catalogues have been selected to perform individual PSHA and have been compared with the results derived from historical and instrumental seismicity. Using R-CRISIS software, this study obtains seismic hazard curves for the main cities in the region, showing the estimated return period for different values of Peak Ground Acceleration (PGA). articles.title: An internally consistent framework for calculating cascading probabilistic earthquake risk and its application to a case study in New Zealand
articles.titleEn: An internally consistent framework for calculating cascading probabilistic earthquake risk and its application to a case study in New Zealand
articles.journal: Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences
articles.abstract: Quantifying the combined effects of earthquakes and their cascading hazards is essential for realistic risk assessment, yet most existing multi-hazard frameworks either neglect the correlations between cascading perils or represent them using simplified assumptions. Dynamic frameworks that explicitly correlate hazard intensities and their uncertainties across cascading perils provide more consistent and physically plausible impact estimates, offering greater value for resilience planning and risk management. This study introduces a probabilistic risk assessment framework that integrates ground shaking, tsunami inundation, liquefaction, landslides, and their combined impacts into a unified modelling approach. The key methodological innovation is a fully correlated Monte Carlo framework that propagates uncertainty from earthquake rupture through sequential hazard models (ground shaking, tsunami, liquefaction, and landslides) to asset damage, preserving the conditional dependence between primary and secondary hazards at every stage of the simulation. This enables physically consistent realization-by-realization estimates of cascading losses rather than combining independently simulated hazards. The framework was tested in Napier, a city of 65 000 inhabitants situated directly above the Hikurangi Subduction Zone (HSZ), New Zealand's largest earthquake source with an estimated maximum credible moment magnitude ( M w ) ∼9.1. A 100 000-year stochastic catalogue of ruptures was generated and applied to ∼30 000 residential buildings, with ground shaking, tsunami inundation, liquefaction severity, and landslide runouts explicitly modelled. Results include damage state and damage ratio metrics for individual and combined perils, allowing attribution of losses across hazards. Ground shaking and liquefaction contribute approximately 60 % of the average annual building damage, with lateral spreading accounting for a further ∼35 %, while tsunami contributes less than 3 % on average. However, for very rare events (return periods >10 000 years), tsunami losses become comparable to those from ground shaking and liquefaction, demonstrating the importance of explicitly modelling cascading hazards. The framework provides decision makers, urban planners, and the (re)insurance sector with actionable metrics to guide resilience investments, refine underwriting, and minimize losses from cascading hazard events.

articles.title: Impact of River Planform and Groyne Lowering on Groyne‐Field Bathymetry
articles.titleEn: Impact of River Planform and Groyne Lowering on Groyne‐Field Bathymetry
articles.abstract: Groyne fields, near‐bank pockets between successive groynes in engineered rivers, act as zones of sediment storage. While groyne‐field bathymetry is known to vary considerably in space and time, the controls on this variability and the consequences of groyne modification thereof remain poorly quantified. Our objective is to quantify the spatial and temporal variability of groyne‐field bathymetry and to assess the impact of groyne lowering on bed‐level change. We combine three data sets from the Waal (Rhine, Netherlands): multibeam bathymetry from approximately 500 groyne fields for spatial analysis; three‐monthly multi‐sensor surveys of three reference fields over three years for temporal dynamics; and multi‐annual repeat surveys across 40 groyne fields to assess the effects of groyne lowering. Wavelet analysis reveals that river curvature controls bathymetry at spatial scales above 2 km: curvature‐driven helical flow causes groyne fields in outer bends to have lower bed levels and steeper transition slopes than those in inner bends. As curvature decreases, local factors such as groyne geometry become comparably important. The greatest bed‐level changes are decimeter scale and occur near groynes, where flow separation drives alternating scour and deposition. Interior groyne‐field changes are centimeter‐scale and often within measurement uncertainty. Contrary to earlier research, peak flows do not consistently induce aggradation. On multi‐year timescales, fields with lowered groynes erode significantly more than unmodified groyne fields, because prolonged groyne submergence exposes the affected groyne fields to higher flow velocities.

articles.title: Integrating surface-active layer-permafrost hydrological processes: A systematic review and research framework
articles.titleEn: Integrating surface-active layer-permafrost hydrological processes: A systematic review and research framework
articles.abstract: Climate warming has accelerated permafrost degradation, leading to significant challenges in water circulation and transformation. Since the early 21st century, especially during the last ten years, permafrost hydrology has garnered substantial attention, yielding a wealth of research outcomes. However, a comprehensive and systematic understanding of the permafrost hydrology remains limited. This study synthesised current knowledge through a comprehensive systematic review and established a Surface-Active layer-Permafrost (SAP) framework that integrated three critical domains: surface hydrological processes, hydrological functions of the active layer, and the hydrological effects of permafrost changes. The SAP framework reveals that permafrost hydrological responses are governed by a causal chain linking climate warming to permafrost degradation, active layer thickening, altered hydraulic properties, enhanced subsurface connectivity, and can ultimately increase baseflow and modified runoff partitioning in many regions. Regarding surface hydrological processes in permafrost regions, this study examined the impacts of freeze–thaw cycles on surface runoff from multiple perspectives, including the influence of slope hydrological processes, river channel dynamics, basin- to regional-scale permafrost hydrology, and the hydrological consequences of thermokarst formation. For hydrological processes within the active layer, the study identified the hydrological role of the active layer, key factors influencing its hydrological behaviour, and the interactions between suprapermafrost water and soil water. Concerning the hydrological impacts of permafrost thaw, this study investigated the transformation dynamics between surface and groundwater in permafrost regions by analysing the effects of climate change through increased baseflow, groundwater recharge, and subsurface runoff. The current state, trends, and challenges in permafrost hydrology research were summarised, and a holistic overview was provided. Finally, future research directions were outlined, emphasising three key areas: the application of novel observational methods, integrated surface-subsurface investigations, and the ecological and environmental impacts of permafrost hydrological changes.

articles.title: AstroComb(v.1.0): non-linear, multi-channel, probabilistic cyclostratigraphic analysis
articles.titleEn: AstroComb(v.1.0): non-linear, multi-channel, probabilistic cyclostratigraphic analysis
articles.abstract: We present a new algorithm for constructing floating astronomical timescales with explicit uncertainty estimates from sedimentary sequences. The method integrates probabilistic spectral analysis with inverse geochronological modelling, applied to ultra-high-resolution, multi-proxy datasets such as core scanning X-Ray Fluorescence (XRF) elemental records. Our framework does not smooth data or impose layer-to-layer dependency, allowing sedimentation rates to vary abruptly at short stratigraphic length scales. By detecting and statistically constraining Milankovitch cycles preserved in stratigraphic signals, the algorithm seeks a floating age-depth model that reconstructs geological time and can be anchored to deliver absolute age assignment, when astronomical tie points and/or radioisotopic ages are available. The resulting timescales enable precise, uncertainty-bounded timing of biostratigraphic zones, geochemical events, and depositional cycles. This approach advances astrochronology by combining cycle detection with formal stratigraphic modelling, while preserving fine-scale depositional variability, offering a reproducible and statistically rigorous framework for dating deep-time records.
