articles.title: Observation operator and detection limits for MODIS and VIIRS Fire Radiative Power products
articles.titleEn: Observation operator and detection limits for MODIS and VIIRS Fire Radiative Power products
articles.abstract: We analyze the MODIS and VIIRS active-fire Fire Radiative Power (FRP) products, suggest an approximation for the FRP detection limit as a linear function of a pixel area, and develop analytical observation operators for both pixel-level and gridded FRP products. We have shown that the collection-6.1 of MODIS has the FRP detection limit at 3.7 MW in case of a nadir retrieval at a clear-sky night. For a daytime sideview, it reaches as high as 40 MW. For VIIRS, the smallest fire reliably detected at night is 0.5 MW. Application of the developed operators for the cross-mapping the MODIS and VIIRS datasets at the pixel/granule level confirmed their consistency. Applying the grid-level operators alongside satellite overpass and weather data, we generated global maps of fire detection probabilities, revealing regional variations. As a global average, probability of detection of powerful fires is 78 % for MODIS (88 % for VIIRS). Variations between regions are large: in some equatorial areas this probability is less than 30 % for MODIS (40 % for VIIRS).

articles.title: Stratospheric aerosol forcing for CMIP7 – Part 2: Volcanic sulfur dioxide emissions
articles.titleEn: Stratospheric aerosol forcing for CMIP7 – Part 2: Volcanic sulfur dioxide emissions
articles.abstract: Explosive volcanic sulfur emissions into the stratosphere form sulfate aerosol particles which are an important driver of climate variability. Volcanic sulfur emissions are required both by climate models using interactive stratospheric aerosol schemes, as well as simpler volcanic aerosol models typically used to provide stratospheric aerosol optical properties for climate models which cannot simulate stratospheric aerosols interactively from precursor emissions. Here we present an upper-tropospheric and stratospheric volcanic sulfur emission inventory covering the period 1750 to 2023, made for phase 7 of the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project (CMIP7). CMIP7 stratospheric aerosol optical properties, presented in a companion paper, are directly derived from this emission inventory for the 1750–1978 pre-satellite period. For the satellite era, the emission inventory is primarily derived from satellite observations. For the pre-satellite period, the inventory is derived from a bipolar ice-core dataset, which captures well eruptions injecting on the order of 10 Tg SO 2 or more, complemented by a high-resolution Greenland ice-core and the geological record, which support the inclusion of eruptions injecting on the order of 0.1–1 Tg SO 2 . We use satellite-era eruptions and older eruptions confidently matched to sulfate deposition records in ice-cores to derive empirical relationships to attribute injection height from SO 2 mass and injection latitude from polar deposition asymmetry when these parameters are missing. The final CMIP7 emission inventory includes 463 explosive eruptions injecting a total of 428.2 Tg SO 2 into the upper troposphere-stratosphere over 1750–2023, corresponding to a mean flux of 1.56 Tg SO 2 yr −1 . For the pre-satellite era, around 25 % of CMIP7 volcanic sulfur emissions originate from small-to-moderate magnitude eruptions, defined here as injecting ≤3 Tg SO 2 , which are not captured in many available ice core arrays. Comparing the CMIP7 inventory with other inventories available for specific time periods, we highlight the large uncertainties characterizing volcanic emissions over the historical period. However, we show that CMIP7 is less biased in terms of the frequency-magnitude distribution of small-to-moderate magnitude eruptions which are largely underestimated in other pre-satellite era inventories. Although the long-term mean emissions associated with these eruptions is consistent with the satellite era in CMIP7, we show that their frequency-magnitude distribution likely remains biased with a lack of small-magnitude eruptions injecting on the order of 0.1 Tg SO 2 , and potentially too many moderate-magnitude eruptions injecting on the order of 1 Tg SO 2 . We discuss other key sources of uncertainties and directions for improvements for the dataset, including the addition of non-sulfur and non-volcanic stratospheric aerosol precursors, as well as needs for operationalizing the dataset production. To support consistent implementation of the dataset in stratospheric aerosol models, we also provide recommendations for the temporal, horizontal, and vertical distribution of emissions associated with each eruption. Modelling groups using the dataset should document in detail any deviation from provided parameter values and recommended emission implementation.

articles.title: FineKarstAGB: a 30 m resolution aboveground biomass dataset for Southwest China derived by upscaling plot-level inventory using sub-meter GaoFen satellite data
articles.titleEn: FineKarstAGB: a 30 m resolution aboveground biomass dataset for Southwest China derived by upscaling plot-level inventory using sub-meter GaoFen satellite data
articles.abstract: Southwest China has emerged as a key global carbon stock due to widespread forest expansion and aboveground biomass (AGB) increases driven by major ecological restoration since 2000, making accurate AGB estimates vital for assessing restoration efficacy. The method takes NFI plot data as ground truth and integrates GaoFen imagery, horizontal structure derived from tree crown segmentation and vertical structure represented by canopy height data. articles.title: Surface sediment grain-size characteristics of the Bohai, Yellow, and East China seas: a comprehensive survey based on unified laser diffraction analysis
articles.titleEn: Surface sediment grain-size characteristics of the Bohai, Yellow, and East China seas: a comprehensive survey based on unified laser diffraction analysis
articles.abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive grain-size dataset comprising 744 surface sediment samples collected from the Bohai Sea, Yellow Sea, and East China Sea – the three major continental shelf seas of China. Samples were obtained over an extended period from 2001 to 2019 using box samplers in accordance with the national marine survey standard (GB/T 12763.8–2007). All samples were analyzed by a Malvern Mastersizer 2000 laser diffraction particle size analyzer following hydrogen peroxide pretreatment for organic matter removal. The dataset provides the full grain-size distribution at 0.25 Φ intervals from −1 Φ to > 10 Φ. The instrument measures directly in micrometres (0.02–2000 µm); we provide two companion data files – one in Φ (phi) scale and one in micrometres (µm) – to accommodate both sedimentological convention and direct instrumental units. The dataset also includes derived Folk–Ward statistical parameters including mean grain size (Mz), sorting coefficient ( σ i ), skewness (Ski), and kurtosis (Kg). Ternary fractions of sand (−1 to 4 Φ), silt (4 to 8 Φ), and clay (> 8 Φ) are also included. Across the dataset, sand content ranges from 0 % to 100 % (mean 40.5 %), silt from 0 % to 76.8 % (mean 41.1 %), and clay from 0 % to 50.3 % (mean 18.4 %). Mean grain size (Mz) ranges from 1.51 to 8.13 Φ (mean 5.23 Φ, corresponding to approximately 27 µm). The dataset is expected to support research on sediment dynamics, paleoenvironmental reconstruction, benthic habitat mapping, and marine engineering across the Chinese continental margin. All data are archived in an open-access repository with a CC BY 4.0 license. The dataset is archived at Science Data Bank and is available at https://doi.org/10.57760/sciencedb.41730 (Duan et al., 2026).

articles.title: HUST-Grace2026s: a high-resolution static gravity field product from GRACE and GRACE-FO observations (2002–2025)
articles.titleEn: HUST-Grace2026s: a high-resolution static gravity field product from GRACE and GRACE-FO observations (2002–2025)
articles.abstract: HUST-Grace2026s is a GRACE-only static gravity field determined by HUST (Huazhong University of Science and Technology). It's determined based on more than 20 years' observation data from GRACE (Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment) and its successor GRACE-FO. The model provides high spatial resolution (up to degree/order 180) for mass distribution monitoring, complementing temporal series like HUST-Grace2024. This study presents the motivation and key outcomes behind our new static gravity field model, HUST-Grace2026s: (1) Merely adding current GRACE-FO observations offers limited improvement to existing GRACE-only models, due to GRACE-FO's current orbital altitude. (2) The application of stochastic model based on postfit residual significantly enhances accuracy, reducing cumulative geoid error by up to 66 % at degree 180 compared to the nominal strategy. (3) The benefit of LRI data on static gravity field determination is strongly tied to the strategy for estimating rate terms. (4) Comprehensive internal and external validation confirms that HUST-Grace2026s achieves higher spatial resolution than unregularized solutions and improves accuracy by over 50 % compared to its predecessor, HUST-Grace2016s. This product serves as a benchmark for long-term mass change studies. The primary model data consisting of potential coefficients representing Earth's static gravity field, together with secular and annual variations. This data set is identified with the following DOI: https://doi.org/10.5880/icgem.2026.001 (Zhou et al., 2026b).

(4) Comprehensive internal and external validation confirms that HUST-Grace2026s achieves higher spatial resolution than unregularized solutions and improves accuracy by over 50 % compared to its predecessor, HUST-Grace2016s. This product serves as a benchmark for long-term mass change studies. The primary model data consisting of potential coefficients representing Earth's static gravity field, together with secular and annual variations. This data set is identified with the following DOI: https://doi.org/10.5880/icgem.2026.001 (Zhou et al., 2026b).

articles.title: Biogeochemical controls on the concentrations and stable isotope compositions of sea-ice particulate organic matters in the Southern Ocean
articles.titleEn: Biogeochemical controls on the concentrations and stable isotope compositions of sea-ice particulate organic matters in the Southern Ocean
articles.abstract: The primary production and zooplankton life cycles in the Southern Ocean synchronize with seasonal sea ice melting, during which particulate organic carbon (POC) and nitrogen (PN), including ice algae, are supplied from sea ice into the water column. To understand carbon flow through food webs in productive marginal ice zones, it is necessary to determine the quantity and quality of organic carbon and nitrogen in sea ice. However, knowledge regarding brash sea ice is scarce, even though it is the predominant form at the Antarctic ice edge. In this study, 102 sea-ice samples were collected from the Indian sector (20–160° E) during summer to clarify variations in isotopic baselines and the potential contribution of sea ice-derived carbon and nitrogen to the water column. The δ 13 C and δ 15 N values of all sea-ice particulate matter samples were -24.6±3.2 ‰ and +1.5±2.2 ‰ (mean ± standard deviation), respectively, showing greater variability compared to those in seawater (-28.8±1.0 ‰ for δ 13 C and -0.5±1.4 ‰ for δ 15 N). We identified correlations of δ 13 C and δ 15 N with organic matter and nutrient concentrations and their ratios (e.g., silicate : nitrate), suggesting that nutrient consumption and organic matter decomposition influenced those isotopic characteristics in sea ice. Using freshwater flux from sea ice melt and the measured sea-ice POC concentrations, the POC supply was estimated to be 4.1±0.3 Tg C yr −1 , equivalent to 14.7±2.8 % of primary production in the marginal ice zone of the studied region. This result suggests that sea ice melt provides significant portion of organic matters potentially supporting Antarctic ecosystems in the seasonal sea ice zone, which could be traced by difference of sea-ice and seawater stable isotope compositions.

articles.title: DMS, MeSH and nanoparticles in semi-controlled deck-borne experiments using Antarctic seawater: on the effect of UV light
articles.titleEn: DMS, MeSH and nanoparticles in semi-controlled deck-borne experiments using Antarctic seawater: on the effect of UV light
articles.abstract: Sulfur-containing volatile organic compounds (VOCs) such as dimethyl sulfide (DMS) and methanethiol (MeSH) are of particular interest among oceanic VOCs emitted by the ocean, both for their central role in the marine sulfur cycle and as potential precursors to secondary aerosol formation. However, the quantification of DMS and MeSH emissions as a function of biological components of the ocean under variable environmental factors are still too scarce for reliable future predictions. In this study we report on measurements of DMS, MeSH and nanoparticle concentrations in the headspace of two on-deck Air-Sea Interface Tanks (ASITs). The cover of one ASIT prevented the transmission of UV light below 380 nm in wavelength and we report on the effect of UV light on fluxes and concentrations. These measurements were carried out near the Antarctic Peninsula during the POLAR-CHANGE campaign in summer 2023. Air–sea fluxes inside the ASITs were always positive, i.e. degassing from seawater to air, with DMS and MeSH fluxes averaging 3.03 pmolm-2s-1 ( F ASIT-DMS ) and 0.64 pmolm-2s-1 ( F ASIT-MeSH ), respectively. DMS emission did not vary significantly between day and night, but the ratio FASIT-MeSH/(FASIT-DMS+FASIT-MeSH) showed a clear maximum at night and a decrease over daytime. Calculated aqueous DMS concentrations showed maxima in the open Southern Ocean north of the Antarctic Peninsula (2.5–3 nM), minima in the Marginal Ice Zone (MIZ) in the Weddell Sea (1 nM) and moderate values along the western coast of the peninsula (around 1.5–2 nM). Bacterial concentrations showed positive correlations with calculated aqueous DMS and MeSH concentrations during two experiments when seawater was held in the ASITs for 2 d. Removal of UV light increased DMS fluxes by 24 % and MeSH fluxes by 58 %. New particle formation occurred only in the absence of UV-light. Interestingly, the highest impact of UV removal, especially on increased MeSH emission, was seen during the night suggesting a lag period between the exposure and the physiological response of the cells. UV light caused slight nanophytoplankton light stress at noon, which negatively affected the short-term growth of nanophytoplankton, especially in open Southern Ocean waters.

articles.title: Macro constraints and local eutrophication shape sediment nitrogen removal in the Eastern China Plain lakes
articles.titleEn: Macro constraints and local eutrophication shape sediment nitrogen removal in the Eastern China Plain lakes
articles.abstract: Eutrophication poses a profound threat to the provisioning of ecosystem services in lakes worldwide. Understanding how eutrophication, alongside other biotic and abiotic factors, drives sediment nitrogen removal is essential for maintaining the intrinsic purification capacity of ecosystems and safeguarding water security. To address this, we conducted a systematic investigation of 17 representative lakes across the Eastern China Plain using 15 N stable isotope tracing, 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing, and metagenomics profiling. This study aims to quantify the contribution of the anammox to nitrogen removal, elucidate the impacts of eutrophication on overall nitrogen removal, and identify the critical biotic and abiotic factors driving these processes. Results revealed that while denitrification was the dominant process across all lakes, anammox made substantial contributions of up to 34.3 %, exhibiting a distinct environmental dependency. Eutrophication significantly amplified both the overall nitrogen removal capacity and the relative contribution of anammox, with local physicochemical properties and microbial communities demonstrating a pronounced joint driving effect on these processes. Notably, the observed decoupling among microbial community structure, functional gene abundance, and nitrogen removal rates highlights a significant discrepancy between genetic potential and active expression. This discrepancy is further manifested by the superior environmental adaptability of functionally redundant denitrifying bacteria compared to narrow ecological niche anammox bacteria. Furthermore, we demonstrate that macro scale factors, including spatial, climatic, and anthropogenic, indirectly drive nitrogen removal by reshaping local water-sediment physicochemical properties, rather than acting as direct determinants of process rates. Collectively, this study enriches our fundamental understanding of nitrogen removal, particularly the anammox process, and its multidimensional drivers in the Eastern China Plain lakes. We advocate that future lake management strategies must rigorously account for the overarching constraints jointly imposed by trophic status, alongside spatial and climatic gradients, to ensure the sustainability of nitrogen purification ecosystem services.

articles.title: Warming vs. browning: a dual mechanism behind net ecosystem production of shallow brown aquatic systems
articles.titleEn: Warming vs. browning: a dual mechanism behind net ecosystem production of shallow brown aquatic systems
articles.abstract: Northern lakes are warming and browning due to increased cDOM inputs, altering water column C:N:P ratios and temperatures that regulate microbial production. Yet the relative importance of warming versus browning, and their combined effects on nutrient stoichiometry and microbial dynamics remain unclear. We experimentally manipulated boreal ponds along a cDOM gradient under ambient and +2 °C warming to quantify impacts on nutrient conditions and microbial production. Browning shifted C:N:P stoichiometry in both total and dissolved pools, with increased C:N and C:P ratios in the total nutrient pools, while reducing inorganic nutrient availability. Despite declining N:P ratios, both pools were strongly carbon-rich and depleted in both N and P. Nutrient-addition assays confirmed NP co-limitation. Browning increased bacterial production, while browning and warming combined reduced primary production, lowering PP:BP ratios. We show that browning -not warming- drives boreal freshwaters toward carbon-rich, N- and P- colimited conditions, while warming and browning together modulate microbial production by amplifying cDOM-driven heterotrophy and suppressing photoautotrophic production. Our study reveals a dual mechanism behind the shifting of brown systems toward heterotrophy. As browning and warming are pervasive trends across Northern lakes, these findings have wide applicability and advance general understanding of how freshwaters respond to ongoing environmental change.

articles.title: Impacts of water advection and CO 2 exchange on the carbon dioxide removal potential of ocean alkalinity enhancement
articles.titleEn: Impacts of water advection and CO 2 exchange on the carbon dioxide removal potential of ocean alkalinity enhancement
articles.abstract: Ocean alkalinity enhancement (OAE) is a carbon dioxide removal strategy with high carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) uptake potential and moderate cost. Long-term implementation has been assessed in modelling studies, but most laboratory experiments have focused on short time frames with strong advection, which may not be representative of natural systems. Hence, the long-term fate of added alkalinity has yet to be fully addressed in laboratory experiments. Furthermore, the role of CO 2 ingassing on overall efficiency is still largely overlooked. In a new setup, six-month experiments were conducted using seawater amended with solid Ca(OH) 2 and Mg(OH) 2 and liquid NaOH, with a constant atmospheric CO 2 supply. Bottles were either kept stagnant or exposed to slow circular advection, yielding gas-transfer-velocity equivalent wind speed of ∼3 m s −1 . All experiments revealed smaller measured increases in total alkalinity than expected, but in the bottles subjected to advection, alkalinity generation was nearly twice as high in some cases and CO 2 ingassing rates were significantly faster. This led to a faster equilibration, decreasing the high pH/low CO 2 period, recently identified as a potential threat to living organisms. The critical alkalinity period (CAP) is introduced here to represent this critical period of altered carbonate chemistry during which secondary calcium carbonate (CaCO 3 ) formation may occur, significantly altering the CDR potential of the approach. CaCO 3 precipitated in most bottles, either as needles when adding Ca(OH) 2 or as broccoli-like structures when adding Mg(OH) 2 . These broccoli-like structures most likely resulted from precipitation on slowly dissolving Mg(OH) 2 particles. After the CAP ended, conditions remained stable and freshly precipitated CaCO 3 did not redissolve. In addition, when NaOH was used as the alkaline feedstock, Mg(OH) 2 flakes were observed but these eventually redissolved in the bottles exposed to advection. The study emphasises the role of water advection on OAE's efficiency and the data presented here may be used to derive lower thresholds for OAE implementation in global models.

articles.title: Reconstruction of the 1989 Laguna del Cerro Largo GLOF: an interdisciplinary understanding of GLOF Impacts
articles.titleEn: Reconstruction of the 1989 Laguna del Cerro Largo GLOF: an interdisciplinary understanding of GLOF Impacts
articles.journal: Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences
articles.abstract: The 16 March 1989, glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF) from Laguna del Cerro Largo in Valle Soler, Aysén, Chile, is one of the largest recent moraine-dammed GLOFs in the region. This interdisciplinary approach reconstructs the GLOF using HEC-RAS 2D and GeoClaw, deriving input parameters from qualitative witness accounts and field methods. Model results are then evaluated through field analysis of sediment deposition, dendrogeomorphic surveys, and radiocarbon dating. Sediment cores reveal distinct clastic layers attributable to the 1989 event and evidence of an earlier outburst flood from the adjacent Laguna Turbio, dated circa 125 ybp. Model results also indicate a substantially higher peak discharge than official reports, impacting subsequent disaster policy decades later. While dendrogeomorphic sampling was hindered by fungal decay in Nothofagus species, the findings highlight both the potential and limitations of interdisciplinary reconstructions of GLOF events in remote, data-scarce environments.

articles.title: Varying Seasonal Runoff Drives the Timing and Volume of Water‐Dependent Recreational Activities in the Sacramento‐San Joaquin Delta
articles.titleEn: Varying Seasonal Runoff Drives the Timing and Volume of Water‐Dependent Recreational Activities in the Sacramento‐San Joaquin Delta
articles.abstract: Climate variations affect access to recreational opportunities through different mechanisms that influence the provisioning of water and ecosystem services. From 2000 to 2022, Northern and Central California experienced extreme climate fluctuations, with alternating multi‐year dry spells and wet years causing highly variable runoff from the Sierra Nevada into the Sacramento‐San Joaquin Delta. This study assesses how these hydroclimatic variations influence regional recreation by analyzing summer activities (boating, day use) alongside winter activities (birding, waterfowl hunting) at state parks and wildlife areas. The objective is to evaluate how monthly visitor volume and timing shift during drought versus wet conditions, distinguishing between activities directly or indirectly dependent on water resources. During summer droughts with critical low runoff, recreational activity declines sharply; boating drops by 65.8% and day use decreases by 13.8% at state park units. Conversely, winter droughts correlate with increased recreational engagement. Critical low runoff is associated with a 23.4% increase in birding observations and a 50.2% increase in waterfowl hunting takes. This winter increase occurs because restricted wetland resources concentrate waterfowl populations, making them more accessible to visitors. Activities directly dependent on water resources, including recreational fisheries, show the highest sensitivity to runoff fluctuations. We also find that visitor spending is highest during critical drought and wet runoff extremes, reflecting winter demand in drought years, and summer demand in the wettest years. These results highlight the vulnerability of water‐dependent recreation and its economic contributions as climate change accelerates the frequency and magnitude of extreme wet and dry cycles.

articles.title: From Hazard to Resource: A Screening‐Level Assessment of Glacial Lake Hydropower Potential and Development Suitability in the Poiqu River Basin, Central Himalaya
articles.titleEn: From Hazard to Resource: A Screening‐Level Assessment of Glacial Lake Hydropower Potential and Development Suitability in the Poiqu River Basin, Central Himalaya
articles.abstract: Climate warming accelerates glacier retreat and glacial lake expansion, creating hydropower opportunities while increasing flood hazards. Despite extensive research on glacial lake hazards, assessments of hydropower potential and development suitability remain limited. Here, we quantify the theoretical hydropower potential of 37 glacial lakes in the Poiqu river basin, central Himalaya, by integrating multi‐scenario climate projections with annual lake water budget reconstruction to estimate hydropower‐relevant inflow across four operational stages during 2025–2100 and by deriving available hydraulic heads through hierarchical river network and topographic gradient analyses. We develop a multi‐criteria framework to evaluate environmental, technical, and economic suitability and prioritize lakes. Across four climate scenarios, basin‐wide mean annual generation is projected at about 212.8 GWhr yr −1 during Stage I (risk mitigation, 2025–2030), followed by about 200.6, 197.0, and 194.3 GWhr yr −1 during Stages II–IV (adaptive generation, 2031–2100), respectively. Paqupuco is identified as the top‐priority site, with annual generation potential of about 14.3 GWhr yr −1 and a suitability score of 80.6. At the regional screening scale, modeled operations could reduce the maximum storage of high‐risk lakes, such as Gangxico and Galongco, to about 71% of their initial capacities. Sensitivity analyses indicate that basin‐wide estimates and leading candidates are broadly stable under the tested water budget and weighting assumptions. By linking hydropower resource assessment with climate‐adaptive hazard governance, this study provides a regional screening framework for jointly evaluating clean energy opportunities and glacial lake outburst flood mitigation in glacierized mountain regions.

articles.title: How Does Extreme Weather Reshape the Time Allocation Among Rural Population? Evidence From China
articles.titleEn: How Does Extreme Weather Reshape the Time Allocation Among Rural Population? Evidence From China
articles.abstract: Extreme weather poses significant threats to rural livelihoods globally. Time allocation serves as a critical short‐term adaptation strategy for rural populations, yet the specific effect of extreme weather on the time allocation remains underexplored. This study examines the effects of four major types of extreme weather—frost, heatwave, heavy rainfall, and drought—on the time allocation among farming, off‐farm work, and leisure activities in rural China. Using an integrated data set combining nationally representative rural household survey data (2019–2023), township‐level geographic information system, and meteorological station observations, this study employs a Tobit random effects model and conducts robustness tests. Results indicate that frost days and heatwave days exhibit U‐shaped relationships with farming hours and inverted U‐shaped relationships with off‐farm work hours. Heavy rainfall shows a positive linear effect on farming hours but a negative linear effect on leisure time. In contrast, drought exhibits no statistically significant effect on time allocation. These effects are heterogeneous across gender, age, and educational attainment. The findings suggest that policy interventions should be tailored according to regional meteorological patterns, with specific attention to the differential vulnerabilities of demographic subgroups to extreme weather.

articles.title: Conservative Spruce Outperforms Acquisitive Larch Under Warming and CO 2
articles.titleEn: Conservative Spruce Outperforms Acquisitive Larch Under Warming and CO 2
articles.abstract: Predicting boreal forest growth is hindered by limited experimental tests on the compounding effects of climate change and atmospheric CO 2 . We integrated regional tree‐ring data with a peatland warming and CO 2 manipulation experiment, including 45 trait measurements, to assess growth responses of two widespread boreal conifers, Larix laricina and Picea mariana , to temperature, vapor pressure deficit (VPD), soil moisture, and elevated CO 2 . L. laricina growth was consistently more climate‐sensitive than P. mariana , increasing strongly with soil moisture and declining slightly with VPD at the regional scale, but responding positively to VPD and temperature—not soil moisture or CO 2 —at the experimental peatland. L. laricina 's acquisitive strategy enhanced water and nutrient uptake, sustaining growth but reducing hydraulic safety. By contrast, P. mariana 's conservative strategy maintained water‐use efficiency and hydraulic resilience without compromising growth. Our results challenge projections of widespread CO 2 fertilization in boreal forests and highlight conservative conifers as potential winners under warming and drying, sustaining growth while maintaining low mortality risk. This dynamic could reshape projections of the boreal carbon sink and its role in global climate feedback.

Our results challenge projections of widespread CO 2 fertilization in boreal forests and highlight conservative conifers as potential winners under warming and drying, sustaining growth while maintaining low mortality risk. This dynamic could reshape projections of the boreal carbon sink and its role in global climate feedback.

articles.title: Impacts of Nuclear War on Human Health From Changed Surface Ultraviolet Radiation
articles.titleEn: Impacts of Nuclear War on Human Health From Changed Surface Ultraviolet Radiation
articles.abstract: Climate model simulations indicate that surface ultraviolet (UV) radiation would change after soot injection into the stratosphere during a nuclear war, due to the competing effects of ozone depletion and aerosol attenuation. Using climate model simulations, we evaluate UV impacts under two scenarios: a regional India‐Pakistan conflict producing 5 Tg of soot and a global U.S.‐Russia war producing 150 Tg. UV enhancements due to ozone depletion substantially shorten safe outdoor exposure time, particularly for individuals with lighter skin types. Applying UV dose‐response relationships to the year 2000 population data, without accounting for direct conflict mortality or famine‐related population loss, the 5 Tg scenarios result in approximately 5,300–9,800 additional skin cancer deaths within 10–15 years and up to 75,000 cumulative excess deaths over the following century. In contrast, strong aerosol attenuation under the 150 Tg scenario initially suppresses surface UV, resulting in about 8,500 fewer skin cancer deaths within 15 years and a maximum cumulative reduction of approximately 17,000 deaths over the following century. These findings demonstrate that nuclear war‐induced changes in surface UV radiation represent a persistent but previously understudied health impact of nuclear war. While skin cancer would not dominate overall mortality following a nuclear war, enhanced cumulative surface UV radiation represents an additional, long‐lasting threat to human health that compounds other global impacts such as climate disruption and food insecurity. The excess UV may also pose negative impacts on animals and plants, including those used for agriculture, which remain to be quantified.

articles.title: Urbanization Amplifies Regional Precipitation Contrasts but not Urban‐Core Precipitation Extremes
articles.titleEn: Urbanization Amplifies Regional Precipitation Contrasts but not Urban‐Core Precipitation Extremes
articles.abstract: Urbanization is often assumed to intensify precipitation and concentrate flood‐relevant extremes in city centers, yet clear observational evidence remains limited. Here, we analyze warm‐season sub‐daily precipitation during 2000–2024 across 20 urban agglomerations and 61 representative cities in China, partitioning built‐up areas into three urban‐intensity zones based on impervious surface fraction. Total precipitation generally increases more rapidly in urban areas than in nearby non‐urban reference regions, with about 75% of urban agglomerations showing faster urban wetting. However, this enhancement is primarily driven by light‐to‐moderate precipitation, for which urbanization effects strengthen systematically from weakly to highly urbanized zones. Quantitatively, urban‐intensity sensitivity is positive for non‐extreme precipitation, with urbanization effects increasing by about 0.1–0.7 mm yr −1 for each 10% increase in impervious surface fraction, but it becomes negative for extremes, decreasing on average by about 0.5–1.1 mm yr −1 . Accordingly, only 20%–25% of urban agglomerations show stronger amplification of extreme precipitation in highly urbanized zones, whereas roughly one‐third show weaker or negative urbanization effects in these zones. These patterns are consistent at the city scale, are more evident at hourly than daily resolution, and are strongest in humid regions. Our results show that stronger urbanization amplifies regional precipitation contrasts but does not systematically amplify precipitation extremes in urban cores, challenging a common assumption in urban flood‐risk assessment and emphasizing the need to distinguish general urban wetting from changes in short‐duration hazardous rainfall.

articles.title: Biodegradable and Non‐Biodegradable Microplastics Drive Divergent Microbial Carbon and Nitrogen Metabolism Regimes in Soil–Plant Systems
articles.titleEn: Biodegradable and Non‐Biodegradable Microplastics Drive Divergent Microbial Carbon and Nitrogen Metabolism Regimes in Soil–Plant Systems
articles.abstract: The accumulation of microplastics (MPs) in soils worldwide has raised concerns about their potential impacts on microbially mediated carbon (C) and nitrogen (N) cycling. However, whether biodegradable and non‐biodegradable MPs differently affect microbial C and N metabolism and coupling, and whether these responses are modulated by co‐occurring plant identity remain uncertain. We combined a meta‐analysis with a controlled pot experiment comparing soil responses under two congeneric plant species exposed to two biodegradable and two non‐biodegradable MPs at doses ranging from 0% to 2% (w/w). In the meta‐analysis, MPs generally increased CO 2 emission and microbial biomass N (MBN), but had no significant overall effect on microbial biomass C (MBC). In the pot experiment, MPs likewise increased CO 2 emission, whereas overall effect sizes of MBC and MBN were nonsignificant. Nevertheless, these overall responses did not capture the distinct patterns of microbial C–N metabolic coordination between MP types. Under biodegradable MPs, tighter MBC–MBN coupling with a dose‐dependent shift toward greater respiratory C loss relative to MBC collectively indicated a maintenance‐associated metabolic pattern. In contrast, MBC–MBN decoupling and stronger MBC–CO 2 coupling under non‐biodegradable MPs indicated a biomass‐linked metabolic pattern. In addition, plant identity modulated these microbial metabolisms in an MP‐type manner, particularly in N‐related processes. These metabolic responses were accompanied with changes in soil property conditions and substrate availability, weakened DOC–DON coupling, and shifts in microbial community structure and life history strategy. RDA‐based hierarchical and variation partitioning and SEM further indicated that modeled soil property pathways were more prominent under non‐biodegradable MPs, while substrate‐related pathways were prominent under biodegradable MPs. Together, the meta‐analysis reveals the general microbial metabolic patterns under MP type, and the pot experiment further reveals how MP type and plant identity jointly influence microbial C–N metabolism through contrasting associations with soil substrates and property conditions.

articles.title: Integrating a global glacier model into local hydrological modeling: Impacts on melt contributions
articles.titleEn: Integrating a global glacier model into local hydrological modeling: Impacts on melt contributions
articles.abstract: Snow and glacier meltwater are critical water resources for mountain regions, yet their accurate representation in hydrological models remains challenging. As climate change alters the timing and magnitude of melt contributions, accurate partitioning between snow and glacier sources becomes increasingly important. To address this challenge, this study couples the hydrological model HBV (as implemented in the Raven modeling framework) with the Global Glacier Evolution Model GloGEM and integrates a snow redistribution scheme for application across 14 glaciated headwater catchments in Switzerland. At this local catchment scale, we investigate whether glacier constraints and the addition of snow redistribution reduce parameter equifinality and increase the reliability of melt contribution estimates. Simulations are evaluated against observed streamflow, gridded snow water equivalent data, and glacier melt data based on observed mass balance. The gravitational snow redistribution algorithm successfully prevents unrealistic high-elevation snow accumulation and improves catchment average SWE simulation performance. Uncoupled HBV configurations outperform coupled HBV-GloGEM setups according to streamflow metrics. However, this superior performance is achieved by simulating glacier melt rates exceeding GloGEM estimates and glacier storage change data by factors of 2–3 in some catchments, effectively using glacier ice to offset precipitation biases in forcing data, which can be critical for climate change impact studies. Within a single model configuration, glacier melt contributions can vary by more than a factor of three among the best-performing parameter sets, and by up to an order of magnitude in weakly glacierized catchments, highlighting severe parameter equifinality. Coupling the HBV model with GloGEM (calibrated using glacier-specific geodetic mass balance) produces glacier melt consistent with observations and substantially improves identifiability of both glacier and snowmelt contributions. Despite lower streamflow performance metrics, glacier melt constraints prevent compensatory errors that would compromise projections as melt dynamics shift under climate change. Applying this framework to future climate scenarios and integrating additional constraints such as snow observations may further improve the reliability of melt contribution projections.

articles.abstract: Chile's hydroclimate exhibits pronounced meridional gradients and strong interannual variability, posing persistent challenges for regime-aware, probabilistic rainfall prediction. articles.title: Unexpected land-surface warming following a relatively limited-forcing hypothetical nuclear war
articles.titleEn: Unexpected land-surface warming following a relatively limited-forcing hypothetical nuclear war
articles.abstract: Nuclear conflicts could ignite intense fires that inject considerable amounts of black carbon (BC) into the upper troposphere and lower stratosphere, with the potential to disrupt global climate. While uncertainties in the BC injection remain large, relatively few modeling studies have explored the climatic response to more limited nuclear exchange between major nuclear powers. Here, we investigate the climate response to a set of relatively limited-forcing scenarios (12 to 24 Tg BC) for nuclear exchanges between the United States and Russia. This corresponds to one-tenth to one-fifth of the forcing strength of typically considered. We use the Canadian Earth System Model version 5, an independent contributor to the worldwide set of Earth System Models that has not been explored previously in this application. Consistent with previous work, decreased downwelling shortwave radiation at the surface drives prolonged surface cooling. Unexpectedly, however, a transient surface warming develops in the first boreal summer following a boreal-winter injection, linked to reduced cooling via net longwave and turbulent fluxes. The transient warming is most pronounced for the lowest forcing cases. Precipitation, which decreases even while the surface warms, is found to be controlled by stabilizing, top-heavy warming. Multi-model assessment of these relatively limited-forcing cases is warranted given their potential impacts.

articles.title: Flood exposure and structure damage under deterministic design-storm and stochastic storm transposition rainfall scenarios: a case study in South Louisiana, USA
articles.titleEn: Flood exposure and structure damage under deterministic design-storm and stochastic storm transposition rainfall scenarios: a case study in South Louisiana, USA
articles.journal: Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences
articles.abstract: Flood hazard maps and damage estimates guide floodplain management, mitigation planning, and engineering design, but they commonly rely on rainfall frequency analysis to define annual exceedance probability (AEP) storms, commonly referred to as design storms. Current engineering practice typically employs spatially uniform design storms derived from point-based gauge statistics; however, this approach suppresses the spatial organization and intensity gradients present in observed storms. Stochastic storm transposition (SST) offers an alternative by preserving the spatial structure of observed rainfall and stochastically repositioning full storm fields across a watershed. This study compares flood exposure and damage produced by Atlas 14 and SST rainfall representations in the Vermilion River Basin, a low-gradient inland–coastal watershed in south-central Louisiana. Although the TP40-adjusted Atlas 14 rainfall depth was larger than the mean basin-average SST accumulation across the 50 realizations (310 mm vs. 238.1 mm), the SST max composite produced substantially greater total structure damage than the baseline Atlas 14 scenario (USD 0.923 billion vs. USD 0.477 billion). Moreover, the comparison identified 11 518 buildings that were inundated in at least one SST realization but not under Atlas 14, representing more than USD 110 million in cumulative structural damage. The divergence between the two approaches is concentrated in mid-elevation urban neighborhoods, where spatial rainfall variability can cross local inundation thresholds that were not crossed under the spatially uniform storm. These results show that, in the VRB, the spatially uniform Atlas 14 design storm missed localized flood exposure that emerged when storm placement and rainfall spatial variability were represented.

articles.title: Runout mechanism of landslides in alluvial basins with emphasis on the impact and erosion effects
articles.titleEn: Runout mechanism of landslides in alluvial basins with emphasis on the impact and erosion effects
articles.journal: Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences
articles.abstract: Landslide runout is a critical factor in risk assessment, and runout distance is the most widely used indicator of mobility. Runout distance is determined both by the landslide's initial conditions and through interactions with erodible substrates, which can affect momentum and inertia by altering basal friction and by increasing overall flow volume, generally increasing runout distance. During erosion, the landslide mass can exert sudden impact forces on the substrate at points where the slope changes abruptly. While erosion effects have been extensively discussed in prior studies, impact forces themselves have been overlooked. Here, we combine fieldwork in SE Tibet, laboratory tests, and numerical modelling to resolve the dynamics and effect of impact loading on landslides in alluvial basins. Impact-loading ring-shear tests and numerical simulations, backed up by field evidence, indicate that impact forces can near-instantaneously generate high excess pore water pressure within a saturated substrate, reducing basal friction of the landslide mass and extending runout. As density and geometry of the impactor determine a landslide impact force, both the impactor and substrate properties, including stiffness and compressibility, control the impact duration. The interplay of these two factors can lead to different landslide runout patterns and mobilities. The findings indicate that the farthest runout does not necessarily occur under the highest impact force; rather, an appropriate impact level exists that most effectively liquefies the substrate. The findings highlight the importance of considering substrate properties for both impact and erosion during landslide runout analyses, particularly those occurring in alluvial basins.

articles.title: Review article: Climate hazards in African cities – knowledge gaps and research needs
articles.titleEn: Review article: Climate hazards in African cities – knowledge gaps and research needs
articles.journal: Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences
articles.abstract: This study conducts a semi-systematic assessment of scientific literature published between 2015 and 2025 to examine the current state of knowledge on climate hazards in African cities. A broad literature search yielded 1832 records, which were conservatively screened to a final sample of 272 articles. The corpus was analysed using quantitative mapping and a qualitative hazard-based expert review. The analysis reveals a rapidly expanding but uneven knowledge base. Research is geographically concentrated, with Central Africa and small and fast-growing secondary cities underrepresented. Flooding and heat-related topics dominate the literature, whereas sea-level rise, windstorms and urban water stress receive comparatively limited attention. Consideration of multiple hazards remains limited and uneven, while explicit analysis of interactions between hazards is rare. Earth Observation is widely used, but its broader potential remains underexploited, while high-resolution urban climate modelling and observations remain limited. Most studies focus on historical or present-day conditions, and few combine future climate scenarios with projected urban growth. Overall, broader geographic and thematic coverage, improved high-resolution observations and urban-scale modelling, and stronger integration of future climate and urban development are needed to provide a more representative evidence base for adaptation and resilience planning in African cities.

articles.title: How Urban–Rural Integration Reshapes the Carbon Source‐Sink Balance: A Carbon Offset‐Based Analysis Revealing Pathways and Scale Effects
articles.titleEn: How Urban–Rural Integration Reshapes the Carbon Source‐Sink Balance: A Carbon Offset‐Based Analysis Revealing Pathways and Scale Effects
articles.abstract: The transition toward carbon neutrality is critically shaped by the management of urban–rural interactions, yet the net carbon consequences of urban–rural integration (URI) remain poorly understood. We systematically assess how URI reshapes the carbon source‐sink balance via an integrated multi‐step analytical approach for 335 Chinese cities (2005–2020). We employ the carbon offset effect (COE)—the net balance between vegetation carbon sequestration (CS) and energy‐related emissions—as a key indicator. We reveal a persistent spatial mismatch between URI advancement and carbon sink capacity, with the national carbon deficit widening from 4.65 to 9.5 Gt CO 2 and the share of emissions offset by vegetation CS falling from 21.98% to 10.41%. Crucially, we identify two competing pathways: A structural optimization pathway associated with improved carbon outcomes, and a spatial squeeze pathway associated with degraded carbon outcomes. The spatial squeeze pathway dominates, as the standardized coefficient of land urbanization level ( β = −0.493) is 6.49 times larger in absolute magnitude than that of the structural optimization pathway ( β = 0.076). The negative association between URI and vegetation COE exhibits scale‐dependent heterogeneity, weakening at higher integration levels and in larger cities, while local synergies between development and carbon sinks are attainable in some key ecological function areas. Our findings reveal the complex relationship between urban–rural transitions and terrestrial carbon dynamics, challenging the assumption that regional integration inherently yields ecological co‐benefits. Incorporating a net carbon‐impact lens into spatial planning is essential to unlock the climate mitigation potential of urban–rural systems, a lesson critical for rapidly urbanizing regions globally.

We reveal a persistent spatial mismatch between URI advancement and carbon sink capacity, with the national carbon deficit widening from 4.65 to 9.5 Gt CO 2 and the share of emissions offset by vegetation CS falling from 21.98% to 10.41%. Crucially, we identify two competing pathways: A structural optimization pathway associated with improved carbon outcomes, and a spatial squeeze pathway associated with degraded carbon outcomes. The spatial squeeze pathway dominates, as the standardized coefficient of land urbanization level ( β = −0.493) is 6.49 times larger in absolute magnitude than that of the structural optimization pathway ( β = 0.076). The negative association between URI and vegetation COE exhibits scale‐dependent heterogeneity, weakening at higher integration levels and in larger cities, while local synergies between development and carbon sinks are attainable in some key ecological function areas. Our findings reveal the complex relationship between urban–rural transitions and terrestrial carbon dynamics, challenging the assumption that regional integration inherently yields ecological co‐benefits. Incorporating a net carbon‐impact lens into spatial planning is essential to unlock the climate mitigation potential of urban–rural systems, a lesson critical for rapidly urbanizing regions globally.

articles.title: Scalable Phase‐Field Implementation of Crack Evolution (SPICE) for Modeling Surface Crevasse Growth and Interaction in Glaciers
articles.titleEn: Scalable Phase‐Field Implementation of Crack Evolution (SPICE) for Modeling Surface Crevasse Growth and Interaction in Glaciers
articles.journal: Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems
articles.abstract: Iceberg calving driven by crevasse propagation is an important source of ice loss from the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets. However, simulating crevasse growth and interaction in 3D, spanning meters to kilometers length scales, remains computationally challenging for high‐fidelity models based on nonlocal continuum damage mechanics and phase‐field fracture approaches. The high computational cost of high‐fidelity models comes from the need to adequately resolve the damage/phase‐field length scale (often meters in scale) within the finite element method to capture complex crevasse patterns and interactions, involving stress redistribution, shielding, and coalescence. To overcome this difficulty, a scalable parallel implementation for crack evolution is developed using the open‐source finite element software FEniCS, which features a novel recursively adaptive mesh refinement (RAMR) algorithm to solve the stress‐based phase‐field fracture model equations in 3D. The RAMR algorithm automatically refines the mesh in the fracture process zones based on the phase field variable and a user‐defined finest cell size to capture crack propagation and coalescence accurately and efficiently. Idealized simulations of kilometer‐scale glacier domains show 13‐ to 45‐fold speedup compared to locally refined meshes, with less than 2% discrepancy in crevasse depth. This computational efficiency enables kilometer‐scale simulations of a field of closely spaced crevasses showcasing arcuate paths and crisscross patterns, resembling field and remotely‐sensed observations of glacier crevasses. The simulations also reveal that crevasse growth is predominantly governed by tensile principal stresses, which are determined by the initial crevasse spacing and margin boundary conditions.

articles.title: Simulating Carbon Emission Dynamics in Agricultural Drainage Ditches: Development and Evaluation of the PCDitch‐Carbon Model
articles.titleEn: Simulating Carbon Emission Dynamics in Agricultural Drainage Ditches: Development and Evaluation of the PCDitch‐Carbon Model
articles.journal: Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems
articles.abstract: With their high abundance in agricultural landscapes, drainage ditches are important components of the global water cycle and potential carbon (CO 2 and CH 4 ) emission hotspots. However, explicit process‐based estimates of carbon emissions from these systems are lacking, with ditch biogeochemical complexity being a major constraining factor. To fill this gap, we developed PCDitch‐Carbon, a carbon emission model, from the well‐established process‐based ditch ecosystem model PCDitch. Our research goals were to (a) identify key parameters that affect carbon emissions using sensitivity analysis, (b) determine the responses in carbon emissions to external nutrient loading using bifurcation analysis and (c) validate the predicted carbon emissions with empirical observations. Sensitivity analysis highlighted hydromorphology, external nutrient and carbon loadings, and ecological states (submerged macrophyte vs. Lemnid dominated vegetation) as key drivers of carbon emissions. Bifurcation analysis showed decreased CO 2 and increased CH 4 emissions with external nutrient loading. Additionally, hysteresis related to ecological state was observed underlying the presence of ecological feedback loops in governing carbon emissions. Modeled emissions reflected empirical observations from 10 ditch systems reasonably well, with higher CH 4 in summer–autumn and lower in winter–spring, as well as lower CO 2 emissions during spring‐summer due to primary production. PCDitch‐Carbon demonstrates the potential of process‐based ecosystem models in understanding and predicting carbon emissions from drainage ditches. Furthermore, this study offers valuable insights into the carbon emission responses in ditch ecosystems over a nutrient loading and depth gradient, thus paving the way for assessing the effectivity of management scenarios in controlling carbon emissions from ditches.

articles.title: The Virtual Biotech: A multi-agent AI framework for therapeutic discovery and development
articles.titleEn: The Virtual Biotech: A multi-agent AI framework for therapeutic discovery and development
articles.abstract: Drug development requires evidence integration across biological scales and modalities, but relevant tools are fragmented. We introduce the Virtual Biotech, an organization of artificial intelligence (AI) agents modeled on a drug-development company, with agentic divisions spanning target discovery, safety assessment, modality selection, and clinical development. We demonstrate its utility at three drug-development decision points. First, more than 37,000 agents annotated outcomes from 55,984 trials and found that drugs targeting cell type–specific genes were 48% more likely to reach market with 32% fewer adverse events. Second, it integrated multimodal evidence to propose a therapeutic strategy in lung cancer. Third, it analyzed a terminated ulcerative colitis trial and inferred potential mechanisms of failure. These results demonstrate that human-guided multi-agent systems can conduct transparent, multiscale analyses to inform therapeutic-development decisions.

articles.title: Safeguarding global terrestrial vertebrate species from future sea level rise
articles.titleEn: Safeguarding global terrestrial vertebrate species from future sea level rise
articles.abstract: Sea level rise (SLR) threatens terrestrial biodiversity, yet its spatiotemporal and species-specific impacts remain unclear. Integrating relative SLR projections across five shared socioeconomic pathways (SSPs) with area of habitat (AOH) maps for 34,120 terrestrial vertebrate species, we project that species exposed to SLR will increase from up to 13,680 in 2050 to 15,324 by 2100, including 57 to 63% of birds, 47 to 52% of mammals, 28 to 36% of reptiles, and 20 to 24% of amphibians. In Southeast Asia, inland inundation areas support high richness. Under SSP5-8.5, species facing >10% habitat inundation surge from 18 in 2050 to 109 by 2100, with reptiles and already threatened species overrepresented. Safeguarding SLR refugia—the noninundated habitats for exposed species—is critical, yet more than 96% lie outside protected areas, which means that early international action is required.

articles.title: Hydromorphological Restoration of Streams Does Not Ensure the Recovery of Ecosystem Functioning
articles.titleEn: Hydromorphological Restoration of Streams Does Not Ensure the Recovery of Ecosystem Functioning
articles.abstract: Ecological restoration is widely expected to recover multiple ecosystem attributes, yet biological structure and ecosystem functioning may respond differently to hydromorphological restoration. Interpreting functional change is further complicated because higher or lower process rates do not inherently indicate recovery; their ecological meaning depends on how degraded and restored conditions compare with an appropriate reference state. We synthesised 582 effect sizes from 66 studies to quantify responses of nine ecosystem functions to hydromorphological restoration of streams and to assess whether changes in biological structure coincided with functional responses. Ecosystem‐function responses varied substantially among processes and baselines. Gross primary production was significantly higher in degraded than in reference streams, illustrating that elevated functional rates do not necessarily indicate reference‐like ecological conditions. Restoration did not consistently reverse degradation‐associated functional differences: denitrification was significantly lower in restored than in degraded streams, whereas nitrate uptake remained significantly lower in restored than in reference streams. Other restored–reference differences were generally weak or uncertain. Functional responses did not differ systematically among broad restoration‐measure categories. Restoration age was associated with changes in gross primary production and denitrification relative to degraded conditions, but none of the functions showed detectable convergence towards or divergence from reference conditions through time. In studies measuring both biological structure and ecosystem functioning, biological responses to restoration were generally positive relative to degraded conditions, whereas functional responses were more variable. However, the available evidence was too uncertain to conclude that biological and functional responses systematically differed. Our synthesis shows that functional recovery cannot be inferred either from restoration‐associated change alone or from concurrent biological recovery. Assessing restoration success therefore requires direct measurements of ecosystem processes and ecologically meaningful reference conditions that reveal whether functional change represents movement towards a process‐specific restoration target.

articles.title: A data-driven method coupling multiple physical constraints for correcting structural errors in groundwater contaminant transport models
articles.titleEn: A data-driven method coupling multiple physical constraints for correcting structural errors in groundwater contaminant transport models
articles.abstract: Model structural errors are pervasive in groundwater contaminant transport modeling under complex environmental conditions, hindering accurate prediction of contamination transport. Data-driven methods (DDMs) coupled with physical constraints provide an effective approach for correcting structural errors and improving prediction. However, in multicomponent reactive transport systems, multiple physical mechanisms must be satisfied simultaneously, whereas existing DDMs have limited capacity to effectively couple multiple physical constraints. To address this challenge, this study proposes a general method for correcting structural errors in groundwater models. A combined likelihood function is constructed and sub-likelihood weights are dynamically updated to effectively couple multiple physical constraints. The method is evaluated using a synthetic three-dimensional tetrachloroethylene reactive transport simulation and a cadmium-phosphate cotransport sand column experiment. These tests systematically assess the effects of coupling single versus multiple physical constraints on structural error correction and predictive performance. The results show that coupling multiple constraints can constrain parameter identification, reduce predictive uncertainty, and more comprehensively improve model predictions. Appropriate physical constraints function analogously to incorporating additional observations. Moreover, coupling multiple physical constraints results in a simpler form of structural error in the calibrated groundwater model, making it easier to characterize, thereby enhancing prediction accuracy and physical consistency. The proposed dynamic updating and stopping criterion of sub-likelihood weights maintains a balance between multiple physical constraints and observations, improving the robustness of parameter identification and constraint enforcement. Overall, the proposed DDM coupled with multiple physical constraints provides a general framework for correcting structural errors in complex groundwater contaminant transport models.

articles.title: Benchmarking convection-permitting climate simulations for hydrometeorological characterizations: a comparative study of WRF-SAAG and observation-based products in Chile
articles.titleEn: Benchmarking convection-permitting climate simulations for hydrometeorological characterizations: a comparative study of WRF-SAAG and observation-based products in Chile
articles.abstract: Over the last few years, significant progress has been made in the development of convection-permitting climate models (CPCMs), especially in improving precipitation estimates in regions with complex terrain. Recently, the South American Affinity Group (SAAG) developed a novel high-resolution dataset – hereafter referred to as the WRF-SAAG dataset – by dynamically downscaling the ERA5 reanalysis using the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model over South America for the period 2000–2021. Here, we evaluate WRF-SAAG outputs across continental Chile and compare them with two widely used gridded meteorological products, CR2MET and RF-MEP, which combine reanalysis data with in situ measurements. In particular, we analyze spatial differences among climatological estimates from the three products, and we assess the quality of daily precipitation and daily maximum and minimum temperature simulations using observations from meteorological stations over the period April/2001–March/2018. We also compare the potential of these climate datasets for hydrological modeling using a conceptual, bucket-style rainfall-runoff model, evaluating the results against streamflow observations, satellite remote sensing (SRS) products, and a snow water equivalent (SWE) reanalysis product. We found that the detection accuracy varied within each Chilean macrozone, with worse performance in the Far North (17.5–26° S) and Patagonia (43.7–56° S). The evaluation of daily precipitation against station observations using Tang's Kling–Gupta efficiency (KGE T ) reveals that all datasets performed better in reproducing precipitation in rainy regions (median KGE T ≥ 0.65 in the Southern macrozone), while in arid areas such as the Near North during summer, the median KGE T was negative. The CR2MET product consistently provided the best performance for extreme precipitation and temperature, partly because it includes information from the stations used for evaluation. Finally, the application of the hydrological model shows that although WRF-SAAG simulations achieved runoff estimations comparable to the best observation-based gridded products (i.e., CR2MET or RF-MEP), with the best results in the southern macrozone they provided relatively lower performance in evapotranspiration (ET) and soil moisture estimates, as well as SWE simulations of competitive quality. More broadly, the results presented here show that, despite some remaining challenges in arid climate regions, kilometer-scale climate models can deliver valuable information for hydrological applications at the daily time scale in Chile.

articles.title: Evaluation of SWOT HR PIXC version D water level time series of small lakes
articles.titleEn: Evaluation of SWOT HR PIXC version D water level time series of small lakes
articles.abstract: The Surface Water and Ocean Topography (SWOT) satellite mission introduces unprecedented 2-D radar interferometry to inland hydrology, aiming to evaluate water bodies down to 0.0625 km 2 . Standard operational products, such as LakeSP, are designed for global applicability but may exhibit suboptimal design choices for particular hydrological regimes. To address this, a customized processing workflow utilizing low-level SWOT L2 HR PIXC vD data was evaluated using 37 small Danish lakes (0.25 to 40 km 2 ) against daily in-situ gauge data from July 2023 to May 2026. The workflow achieves a median root-mean-square error (RMSE) of 5.57 cm and a Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC) of 0.91, similar to LakeSP. Crucially, this approach retains a median of 125 valid timestamps per lake compared to 60 timestamps preserved by the filtered LakeSP product, effectively doubling the temporal resolution and enabling the capture of higher-frequency hydrological variations. Additionally, we find indications that SWOT's PIXC data contains time-varying residual roll-errors over Danish lakes that affect ca 18 % of all passes with more than 10 observed lakes covering Denmark.

articles.title: Attribution of Changes in European Flood and Drought Magnitudes to Climatic and Socioeconomic Drivers
articles.titleEn: Attribution of Changes in European Flood and Drought Magnitudes to Climatic and Socioeconomic Drivers
articles.abstract: Hydrological extremes display long‐term trends and natural oscillations in response to climatic and socioeconomic factors. Knowing how and why these extremes are shifting is crucial for increasing water resilience in Europe. This work analyses trends in floods and droughts in European catchments between 1951 and 2020. Using the OS LISFLOOD hydrological model and non‐stationary extreme value analysis, we disentangle the effects of dynamics in climate, encompassing climate variability and climate change, land use, water abstraction and reservoirs on river flow extremes. Our results reveal spatial and temporal variations in magnitude of hydrological extremes. Land use changes have generally increased flood and drought hazards, while water demand primarily intensified droughts. Reservoirs, conversely, have decelerated the hydrological cycle. Our work delivers insights into the intricate connections between climate, society, and water in European river basins, enabling the development of effective strategies for enhancing resilience to extreme water events under global change.

articles.title: Non‐Linear Increases of Soil Carbon Stocks and Turnover Along Alpine Greening Gradients on Different Bedrocks
articles.titleEn: Non‐Linear Increases of Soil Carbon Stocks and Turnover Along Alpine Greening Gradients on Different Bedrocks
articles.abstract: Alpine ecosystems are experiencing warming, leading to alpine greening—an upward migration and enhanced productivity of vegetation. Although soils represent the largest carbon (C) stocks in these ecosystems, impacts of greening on soil organic carbon (SOC) dynamics remain unknown, especially in the high alpine zone. We measured SOC stocks, quality and radiocarbon ( 14 C) based turnover rates along elevation gradients from (sub)alpine forests to periglacial zones on three bedrock types, representing trajectories of changes in climate and vegetation and weathering regime. Data were linked to SOC stabilizing pedogenic oxides (PO) to assess the potential of soils to sequester C upon alpine greening. Results show pronounced decreases in SOC stocks (from 10 to 1 kg C m −2 ) and increases in 14 C‐based turnover times (from decades to millennia) with increasing elevation. This pattern followed a non‐linear sigmoidal function with a threshold at the vegetation line where grassland transitions to the nival zone. High alpine soils showed low SOC:PO ratios, indicating low C saturation and a high capacity to stabilize SOC on reactive minerals. However, negligible 14 C‐derived carbon inputs suggest that low vegetation productivity constrains SOC sequestration in these soils. In contrast, towards lower elevation with a warmer climate, grassland soils receive higher C inputs, but appear more C saturated, leading to greater SOC turnover but little SOC stock changes. Bedrock influenced SOC dynamics with approximately 50% smaller SOC stocks and faster turnover rates in dolomitic than in siliceous soils, due to slower weathering and lower SOC stabilization. Using elevation as a space‐for‐time substitution, we infer that SOC sequestration under alpine greening will be confined to areas around the vegetation line, with parent material influencing the magnitude of C uptake. Future projections of SOC dynamics should account for vegetation shifts and bedrock‐driven stabilization to constrain the role of alpine soils in land carbon‐climate feedbacks.

articles.title: Cold activates a BH2 metabolic network promoting longevity and proteostasis
articles.titleEn: Cold activates a BH2 metabolic network promoting longevity and proteostasis
articles.abstract: Moderately cold temperatures extend lifespan and promote health across species 1–3 , yet the molecular mechanisms underlying these benefits remain unclear. Here we define a metabolite-driven, multi-tissue signalling system that links cold temperature to enhanced longevity and proteostasis in Caenorhabditis elegans . Cold temperature upregulates the biopterin-synthesis enzyme CAT-4 (GCH1 in humans), increasing production of dihydrobiopterin (BH2), a transportable reservoir for the bioactive cofactor tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4). BH2 is produced in muscle and transported to distal tissues, including the intestine and neurons, where it is converted into BH4 by the salvage enzyme DHFR-1. BH4 functions as an essential cofactor for phenylalanine hydroxylase PAH-1, promoting tyrosine synthesis and extending lifespan. This BH2–BH4 axis also prevents disease-related protein aggregation and subsequent neuronal dysfunction during ageing. Importantly, increasing BH2 synthesis specifically in muscle is sufficient to promote longevity and suppress pathological protein aggregation in distal tissues, even at normal or elevated temperatures. In human cells, BH2 or tyrosine supplementation reduces aggregation of polyQ-expanded proteins associated with Huntington’s disease, as well as mutant variants of TDP-43 and FUS that cause amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Together, these findings identify BH2 as a cold-induced metabolite of which the synthesis, intertissue transport and conversion into bioactive BH4 preserve organism-wide proteostasis and extend lifespan.

Importantly, increasing BH2 synthesis specifically in muscle is sufficient to promote longevity and suppress pathological protein aggregation in distal tissues, even at normal or elevated temperatures. In human cells, BH2 or tyrosine supplementation reduces aggregation of polyQ-expanded proteins associated with Huntington’s disease, as well as mutant variants of TDP-43 and FUS that cause amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Together, these findings identify BH2 as a cold-induced metabolite of which the synthesis, intertissue transport and conversion into bioactive BH4 preserve organism-wide proteostasis and extend lifespan.

articles.title: Drought and disease trigger novel interactions among top predators
articles.titleEn: Drought and disease trigger novel interactions among top predators
articles.abstract: Interactions among species are increasingly recognized as key determinants of climate change impacts on ecosystems 1–5 . However, we know little about how climatic perturbations affect interactions among top vertebrate predators. Here we show that, when an emergent disease caused the decline of shared prey (rabbits), after decades of neutral co-existence a mammalian carnivore (lynx) started to prey heavily on a top predatory raptor (kites). These predation bouts occurred exclusively under drought conditions and when lynx found rabbit remains under the raptor nests, consistent with the removal of a potential competitor. Drought-induced lynx predation depressed lifetime reproductive success and triggered territory abandonment and dispersal by the raptor, suggestive of a new arms race among predators. A reduction in raptor abundance was associated with an increase in an insectivorous bird (a small owl), showing that the new interaction had the potential to reach lower trophic levels. These results underline the importance of diet flexibility and mobility as important mediators of resilience to stressors. In the future, synergistic effects of multiple anthropogenic stressors may reshape the interactions and ecological roles of many apex predators, with potential cascading consequences for whole ecosystems. A key to forecasting the future impact of global change may reside in understanding how behavioural flexibility and interacting keystone species respond to interacting shocks.

articles.title: Climate Change Experienced by Life on Earth—Drivers and Mechanisms of Future Trends in Microclimates
articles.titleEn: Climate Change Experienced by Life on Earth—Drivers and Mechanisms of Future Trends in Microclimates
articles.abstract: Microclimate, the climate directly experienced by organisms, is crucial for understanding ecological responses to climate change, yet its long‐term dynamics and the drivers of decadal microclimate changes remain underexplored in ecology and global change biology. Microclimate changes do not necessarily track macroclimate trends. Changes in meteorological conditions (e.g., cloud cover, wind patterns) and vegetation dynamics (e.g., canopy opening, desertification in drylands, shrub encroachment in the tundra) associated with climate change can lead to locally divergent microclimate trends, thereby altering spatial variability. Understanding and quantifying how macroclimate change translates to fine‐scale microclimate change experienced by organisms, populations and communities is therefore essential for predicting ecological responses to global environmental change. This review examines how macroclimate change drives microclimate changes as experienced by life on Earth—and how these micro‐scale changes may, in turn, feed back into the regional and global climate system. Our primary focus is on near‐surface air and soil temperature—due to their relevance to most terrestrial organisms and ecosystem processes. The review is structured around three pathways of microclimate changes: (I) direct effects of changes in meteorological conditions, (II) indirect effects via vegetation changes, and (III) feedbacks between microclimate and climate change. Using three mechanistic model simulations in real‐world landscapes, we illustrate and quantify the key mechanisms that lead to divergent warming trends. We show that microclimate change emerges from interacting atmospheric, land‐surface, and biophysical processes, which can differ substantially across space and time. Predicting future microclimates therefore requires accounting for these processes and their temporal dynamics. By providing an accessible synthesis of these processes, this review aims to strengthen links between ecology and atmospheric science and improve our understanding of how climate change translates into microclimatic conditions relevant to life on Earth.

articles.title: Amazon carbon emissions driven by human actions amplified by droughts
articles.titleEn: Amazon carbon emissions driven by human actions amplified by droughts
articles.abstract: The Amazon carbon sink is weakening as deforestation 1–5 , rising tree mortality 6–8 and climate change disrupt the climatic conditions that sustain a humid tropical forest 9–11 . Forest loss reduces precipitation, increases temperatures and lengthens the dry season, driving higher carbon emissions 1–4,11,12 . Climate stress is stronger in more deforested regions, rendering forests progressively more flammable 1,9,13 . Large-scale climate events, such as El Niño, further amplify regional climate impacts 9,14–17 . Here we present an analysis of 15 years of Amazonian carbon fluxes derived from atmospheric CO 2 measurements. We determine a carbon balance of 0.32 ± 0.08 PgC yr −1 , with fires acting as the dominant source (0.40 ± 0.07 PgC yr −1 ) and forest uptake becoming increasingly unable to offset emissions. Furthermore, we investigate key drivers of the carbon emissions of Amazonia and identify three distinct year groups. Group 1 (2011–2014, 2017 and 2018) represents the role of the Amazon in the global carbon balance (0.11 ± 0.08 PgC yr −1 ) during wetter years with low human activity, such as deforestation, biomass burning and degradation. Group 2 (2019–2022) represents Amazon carbon emissions (0.43 ± 0.13 PgC yr −1 ) from human activities (mainly deforestation and degradation) during years with low climatic stress. Group 3 (2010, 2015, 2016, 2023 and 2024) has the highest carbon emissions (0.49 ± 0.07 PgC yr −1 ) and comprises warm and dry years (high climate stress), such as El Niño and the warming of the Tropical North Atlantic Ocean, associated with biomass burning.
