articles.title: Benchmarking conditioners in Liang–Kleeman Information Flow: application to land–atmosphere interactions in humid forests
articles.titleEn: Benchmarking conditioners in Liang–Kleeman Information Flow: application to land–atmosphere interactions in humid forests
articles.abstract: The Liang–Kleeman Information Flow (LKIF) framework has been increasingly used to identify causality in Earth–system dynamics in recent years. Yet, uncertainties remain regarding how the causal graph changes when mediators and confounders (conditioners) are introduced, i.e., divergence between the bivariate and conditioned forms. A controlled synthetic experiment shows that LKIF preserves correct causal directions under hidden confounding, while differences between bivariate and multivariate estimates still occur. We characterize these differences using time-varying LKIF and introduce several quantifiers, including Conditioner Dominance Index, Moderation Gain, Conditioning Pressure, and Convergence Rate, to evaluate the contributions of conditioners. This is illustrated in an application to soil moisture (SM) and vapor pressure deficit (VPD) couplings with vegetation (leaf area index (LAI) and gross primary productivity (GPP)) in humid forest regions of Southeast China and the Amazon Basin, using satellite-derived and reanalysis data over 1981–2018. We find that the influence of SM on LAI remains consistently stable and shows little sensitivity to the selected conditioners, whereas its influence on GPP and that of VPD on vegetation exhibit substantial divergence between bivariate and multivariate estimates. This divergence peaks under compound dry–hot conditions, with VPD and temperature emerging as dominant conditioners. These results demonstrate that bivariate and multivariate LKIF can yield markedly different conclusions across time and space, especially under compound environmental stress. More importantly, even for the same variables in a causal graph, the same conditioners can affect the temporal evolution of the causal relationships very differently at different locations. This highlights how stationary assumptions may oversimplify causal structure by masking relevant temporal transitions, particularly under compound environmental stress.

articles.title: Improving AquaCrop Root‐Zone Soil Moisture by Assimilating SMAP Surface Soil Moisture
articles.titleEn: Improving AquaCrop Root‐Zone Soil Moisture by Assimilating SMAP Surface Soil Moisture
articles.journal: Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems
articles.abstract: Root‐zone soil moisture (RZSM) strongly controls crop development in process‐based crop models, yet most satellite missions observe only near‐surface moisture. We propose a framework to assimilate soil moisture active passive (SMAP) Level‐2 surface soil moisture retrievals into AquaCrop to improve RZSM over European croplands (0.1° resolution, 2015–2023). We assimilate either these SMAP retrievals directly, or exponentially filtered SMAP retrievals optimized for specific target depths (0–30, 0–60, and 0–100 cm), always bias‐corrected using seasonally varying cumulative distribution function matching within an ensemble Kalman filter. AquaCrop's cascading, threshold‐based soil water balance exhibits much weaker short‐term vertical coupling than in situ observations, limiting the downward propagation of surface‐only updates. Consistent with this behavior, assimilation of both surface retrievals and exponentially filtered SMAP data improves topsoil moisture (0–30 cm), while subsoil (30–100 cm) and RZSM (0–100 cm) improve most when assimilating exponentially filtered observations that embed temporal persistence of deeper soil depths. Best overall RZSM performance is obtained by assimilating SMAP data exponentially filtered to a target depth of 0–60 cm, yielding widespread increases in anomaly correlation against in situ observations. Improvements in soil moisture translate only weakly and inconsistently to vegetation space: updated soil moisture better explains interannual variability in satellite vegetation indicators but improvements in canopy cover and biomass simulated by AquaCrop remain limited. These results indicate that while exponential‐filter‐based soil moisture assimilation robustly improves deeper moisture, joint assimilation of soil moisture and vegetation observations is needed to better constrain soil–plant coupling and ensure that soil moisture corrections propagate more effectively into crop growth predictions.

articles.title: Investigating Cloud–Radiation Error Compensations Stemming From Climate Model Calibration
articles.titleEn: Investigating Cloud–Radiation Error Compensations Stemming From Climate Model Calibration
articles.journal: Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems
articles.abstract: Compensating errors are an obstacle to the development of climate models. We wonder if systematic errors in simulated cloud properties might result from forced error compensation due to targeting top‐of‐atmosphere radiative fluxes in the tuning process while using an inaccurate radiative transfer (RT) parameterization. Here, we investigate the extent to which parametric and structural errors in state‐of‐the‐art RT models might be offset by errors relating to cloud properties, and under what circumstances. For this we run tuning experiments with a Single‐Column version of a climate Model (SCM), with and without a parameterization of 3D radiative effects of clouds, targeting reference solar fluxes calculated on Large‐Eddy Simulation cloud fields. In a first set of tuning experiments, the parameters that control cloud geometry in the radiative transfer code are tuned assuming perfect cloud profiles. Compensation mechanisms are found between cloud geometry effects, notably between cloud vertical overlap and 3D effects. In a second set of experiments, cloud geometry parameters are set to nominal values, and free parameters of the boundary layer and cloud parameterizations are tuned, still targeting radiative metrics. We found that, when 3D effects are neglected in these experiments, reasonable fluxes are obtained only at the expense of overestimated cloud fractions, partly compensating for underestimated cloud reflectivity at low sun. Targeting mean solar‐angle fluxes instead of detailed ones removes this mechanism entirely. This study both enlightens some compensation errors specific to cloud–radiation interaction and illustrates more generally how the tuning tool can be used to study and quantify compensating errors.

articles.title: Political affiliation impacts climate attention and choice beyond extreme weather exposure
articles.titleEn: Political affiliation impacts climate attention and choice beyond extreme weather exposure
articles.abstract: Political polarization and increasing exposure to extreme weather can shape public engagement with climate change, yet the underlying psychological mechanisms remain unclear. In this Registered Report, we examine how political affiliation, extreme weather exposure and subjective attribution influence climate-relevant information search and decision-making in a US sample ( N = 1,451). We combined a process-tracing paradigm within an incentivized decision task involving real carbon emissions with objective data on extreme weather exposure. Democrats attended more to carbon emission information and made more pro-climate choices than Republicans, with no evidence of moderation by objective extreme weather exposure. The subjective attribution of extreme weather to climate change was associated with greater attention to carbon information, more pro-climate choices and moderated the effects of exposure on both outcomes. These findings highlight the importance of political affiliation in climate-relevant decision-making and suggest that extreme weather effects depend less on exposure itself than on how these experiences are interpreted.

articles.title: Palaeoclimate constraints narrow uncertainty in future Arctic winter sea ice projections
articles.titleEn: Palaeoclimate constraints narrow uncertainty in future Arctic winter sea ice projections
articles.abstract: Arctic sea ice decline has been observed across all seasons and is projected to continue in the future. Relative to historical observations, climate models show their largest biases and uncertainties during winter, when ice cover strongly regulates air–sea heat exchange, ocean mixing and atmospheric circulation. Palaeoclimate records offer opportunities to evaluate model performance beyond the historical period, but applications have remained largely qualitative. Here we compile an Arctic-wide database of mid-Holocene (5–7 thousand years ago) biomarkers to assess sea ice simulations of this past warm period. Using a recently developed proxy system model, we present a Bayesian palaeoclimate model weighting scheme that refines the multi-model mean winter sea ice extent through fully quantitative proxy-model comparisons, accounting for model interdependence and non-stationary proxy seasonality. We demonstrate that, by adjusting the contribution of each model to the ensemble mean based on proxy evidence, model weights can eliminate biases and reduce uncertainties by 85%, to the level of interannual variability. Weighted projections using the same climate models indicate that future winter sea ice extent may be nearly 1 million km 2 lower than prior estimates across forthcoming decades and possible emissions scenarios, with broad implications for Arctic ecosystems, mid-latitude weather, and cryosphere stability.

articles.title: Kilometer‐Scale Modeling of Atmospheric River Precipitation Using the Regionally Refined SCREAM Model
articles.titleEn: Kilometer‐Scale Modeling of Atmospheric River Precipitation Using the Regionally Refined SCREAM Model
articles.journal: Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems
articles.abstract: This study evaluates kilometer‐scale simulations of atmospheric river (AR) precipitation using the Simple Cloud Resolving E3SM Atmosphere Model (SCREAM). Four AR events that cause flooding and impact the Puget Sound basin in the U.S. Pacific Northwest (PNW) are simulated using SCREAM with a regional refined mesh (RRM) at 3.125 km over the PNW within a global domain at 25 km resolution. Two SCREAM configurations are evaluated that differ only in their representation of ice‐cloud fraction: the original version (SCREAMv0) uses a relative humidity‐based formulation, whereas the revised version (SCREAMv0+) uses the cell‐averaged ice mass mixing ratio. For all AR cases, SCREAMv0+ simulates stronger lower‐level wind, more precipitable water, and increased moisture flux than SCREAMv0, aligning more closely with ERA5 reanalysis. With realistic large‐scale circulation, SCREAMv0+ increases precipitation over the Cascades and decreases it over the Coastal Range, leading to a closer resemblance of the spatial rainfall distribution according to multiple observational products. SCREAMv0+ shows a deeper layer of cloud ice and mixed‐phase hydrometeors than the SCREAMv0 simulations. It is likely that an altered latent heat release, caused by changes in the representation of ice‐ and mixed‐phase mass ratios, causes a large‐scale circulation response that eventually affects the precipitation distribution. Sensitivity experiments confirm these changes are mainly driven by how ice‐cloud fraction interacts with microphysics. Results show that altering cloud macrophysics can significantly change the connection between microphysics, diabatic heating, and large‐scale circulation in kilometer‐scale models. These findings emphasize the importance of cloud mixed‐phase processes in AR precipitation and demonstrate how regionally refined models like SCREAM can well simulate cold‐season extreme rainfall in complex terrain.

articles.title: Diffusion‐Based Reconstruction of Western North Pacific Surface Winds From CYGNSS for Tropical Cyclone Analysis
articles.titleEn: Diffusion‐Based Reconstruction of Western North Pacific Surface Winds From CYGNSS for Tropical Cyclone Analysis
articles.journal: Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems
articles.abstract: Sea surface wind retrieval under extreme weather conditions is constrained by the sparse and irregular spatiotemporal sampling of Global Navigation Satellite System Reflectometry (GNSS‐R). This study presents a probabilistic wind field reconstruction framework for the Western North Pacific using Score‐Based Data Assimilation (SDA). A diffusion model trained on historical wind analyses serves as a statistical prior, and sparse Cyclone Global Navigation Satellite System (CYGNSS) observations constrain the reverse diffusion process to draw samples from an approximate posterior. Track‐segment withholding (80% input, 20% verification), additionally excluding verification cells containing input observations, yields a case‐averaged Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) of 1.637 m/s. In Tropical Cyclone (TC) scenarios, for cases with analysis‐box CYGNSS coverage above 10%, the reconstruction reduces the inner‐core intensity bias of both gridded references (the fifth‐generation European Centre for Medium‐Range Weather Forecasts reanalysis by 78.4%, and the Cross‐Calibrated Multi‐Platform analysis—its own training prior—by 70.1%) with lower RMSE than the reanalysis but slightly higher RMSE than the multi‐platform analysis. Furthermore, the framework provides informative pixel‐level uncertainty estimates that are under‐dispersed relative to withheld CYGNSS observations, with the spread correlating with the reconstruction error. These results indicate improved mean intensity estimates in the higher‐coverage subset, with performance still dependent on inner‐core sampling.

Furthermore, the framework provides informative pixel‐level uncertainty estimates that are under‐dispersed relative to withheld CYGNSS observations, with the spread correlating with the reconstruction error. articles.title: Progressive oxidative weathering raised sub-arc mantle fugacity on the Archaean Earth
articles.titleEn: Progressive oxidative weathering raised sub-arc mantle fugacity on the Archaean Earth
articles.abstract: In the modern Earth, sub-arc mantle oxygen fugacity is intrinsically associated with addition of sulfur species by slab fluids. However, it is unclear to what extent recycling of volatiles controlled redox changes of the sub-arc mantle in the early Earth. Here we use sulfur K-edge micro-X-ray absorption near-edge structure spectroscopy to measure the relative abundances of S 6+ , S 4+ and S 2− in apatite inclusions hosted by geochemically characterized and dated zircons from sub-arc sanukitoid magmas that span 3.4 billion years of Earth’s geological history. The sub-arc mantle shows marked increase in oxygen fugacity between 3.4 and 3.0 billion years ago (Ga). It is substantially more oxidized than unaltered ambient upper mantle, a characteristic that cannot be explained by fractionation, degassing or intrinsic mantle processes. We propose that progressive oxidative weathering enhanced the proportion of oxidized sulfur recycled to mantle wedge sources, establishing feedback between subduction of surface materials and incrementally oxidized arc magmatism. Early subduction involving inorganic oxidation and ‘whiffs’ of oxygen between 3.4 and 2.7 Ga may have regulated an early increase in fugacity of the sub-arc mantle before the Great Oxidation Event, matching similar conditions to the modern Earth by 2.1 Ga.

articles.title: Impact of Spatially Continuous Urban Surface Properties on Summertime and Heatwave Simulations: A Multi‐City Analysis
articles.titleEn: Impact of Spatially Continuous Urban Surface Properties on Summertime and Heatwave Simulations: A Multi‐City Analysis
articles.journal: Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems
articles.abstract: Urban areas are unique in form, function, and fabric, and representing them in process‐based models requires, among other things, prescribing facet‐level morphological and radiative properties, which vary widely. Most urban canopy models (UCMs) prescribe these by density class or local climate zone (LCZ), assigning identical values across broad regions or worldwide. Global km‐scale, facet‐level urban property data sets have recently emerged, but are seldom applied in regional modeling. Here, we incorporate one such data set, U‐Surf, into the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model, modifying it for WRF's multi‐layer UCM and releasing it as U‐Surf‐WRF. Considering 13 US cities, U‐Surf‐WRF parameters vary more between LCZs than default WRF parameters, with consistently lower impervious fraction. To determine the effects of using U‐Surf‐WRF, we conduct high‐resolution WRF summertime seasonal and recent heatwave simulations for these 13 cities using default and U‐Surf‐WRF parameters. Either prescribed by LCZ or for each grid point, using U‐Surf‐WRF usually yields more accurate surface temperatures. It generally decreases modeled urban air temperature and increases modeled urban humidity, yielding lower heat and dry islands. Decomposing the impact of each U‐Surf‐WRF variable, we find that while albedo can impact daytime simulations, especially for air temperature, morphology and impervious fraction are most relevant, especially for surface temperature. This study demonstrates the impact of city‐specific, facet‐level urban properties in urban‐resolving numerical weather simulations, with remaining gaps against observations demonstrating other challenges in representing cities in process‐based models. Conversely, in WRF simulations with poorly constrained parameters, we suggest caution interpreting the magnitude and spatial distribution of urban signals.

articles.title: From paper to proof: revealing Congo Basin warming through rescued climate archives
articles.titleEn: From paper to proof: revealing Congo Basin warming through rescued climate archives
articles.abstract: The Congo Basin in Central Africa remains one of the few regions globally where the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change has neither assessed changes in hot extremes and extreme precipitation since the 1950s nor attributed such changes to anthropogenic influences, primarily due to the sparsity of in situ observational data. Although extensive daily weather records exist, spanning from the 1900s to the early 2000s and covering numerous stations across the basin, the majority of these remain archived on paper, limiting their accessibility for climate analysis. Here we present and analyse over 1 million temperature and precipitation observations from 37 weather stations in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, which have until now been unavailable to the research community. To produce this dataset, we first digitized (imaged) 9885 paper sheets stored in local archives during two dedicated field campaigns. We subsequently apply an improved version of the MeteoSaver software (version 1.1) to transcribe the imaged sheets, yielding daily time series of maximum, minimum, and average temperatures, precipitation, as well as dry bulb and wet bulb temperatures measured at three times per day (06:00, 15:00, and 18:00 local time). After quality control, analysis of multi-decadal temperature data across the basin reveals a consistent and accelerating warming signal since the 1960s, characterized by a warming shift in the distribution of daily maximum, minimum, and average temperatures with each successive decade. Median trends across 21 of the 37 stations with sufficient data availability are 0.22, 0.10, and 0.15 °C per decade for daily maximum, minimum, and average temperatures, respectively, corresponding to approximately 0.7, 0.3, and 0.5 °C of warming during the 1961–1990 period. We further find an increasing frequency of hot extremes and a decreasing frequency of cold extremes with each successive decade, with the most recent decade exhibiting nearly twice as many hot days per year and fewer cold days compared to the earliest decade. Analysis of precipitation at three stations with sufficient data indicates an increased frequency of heavy precipitation events at two stations and no substantial change at the third; however, limited spatial coverage due to data availability restricts broader conclusions for the DRC. Overall, this analysis of rescued weather data from Central Africa highlights the urgent need to close the knowledge gap on climate trends in the Congo Basin, one of the world's most data-sparse yet climatically significant regions.

articles.title: A Catchment‐Based Global Model of River Discharge and Flow Velocity for Earth System Models
articles.titleEn: A Catchment‐Based Global Model of River Discharge and Flow Velocity for Earth System Models
articles.journal: Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems
articles.abstract: The representation of river flows in Earth System Models (ESMs) is crucial for understanding water resources availability, contaminant transport, and the impacts of climate change on river systems. In this study, we introduce a global runoff routing model founded on hydraulic geometry principles and hydrologic catchments, specifically designed for integration with ESMs. To simulate river dynamics, the model capitalizes on (a) the river network topology defined by the Pfafstetter coding system, (b) hydraulic geometry principles that connect river discharge to flow velocity, and (c) calibration using more than 2.7 million intermittent field measurements of flow velocity in the contiguous US (CONUS). The model is shown to produce reasonably accurate natural daily river discharge over CONUS except within some arid regions and the region adjacent to the Great Lakes, where streamflow is strongly impacted by reservoir management and by the natural buffering behavior of the large lakes themselves. The average correlation coefficient for discharge (vs. in situ measurements) is 0.80 for tested major rivers over CONUS except in arid regions and the Great Lakes. A unique feature of the model is its ability to simulate flow velocity with realistic magnitudes, standing it in good stead for tracer tracking and water management applications.

articles.title: An Online Moisture Tagging Framework for Detrainment of Convective Hydrometeors and Associated Precipitation in Convection‐Permitting Models
articles.titleEn: An Online Moisture Tagging Framework for Detrainment of Convective Hydrometeors and Associated Precipitation in Convection‐Permitting Models
articles.journal: Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems
articles.abstract: Convective detrainment is an important process in mesoscale convective systems (MCSs) that strongly influence adjacent stratiform clouds and precipitation. However, it remains difficult to quantify convective detrainment in numerical models. In this study, we develop an online convection identification and water vapor tracer (WVT) framework based on the Eulerian WVTs coupled with Weather Research and Forecasting convection‐permitting model. Convection is identified using radar reflectivity, and two types of tracers are introduced to track water species and precipitation within convective regions and those detrained from them, which can be distinguished from those newly generated in the stratiform areas. The framework is applied to both an idealized case and a real case. In the idealized simulation, the framework captures the convective detrainment and its associated precipitation during the lifecycle of convective systems featured by rapid evolution in location and structure. In the real case, the framework demonstrates distinct temporal variations in the intensity and area coverage of stratiform precipitation produced by convective detrainment. Both the ice‐ and liquid‐phase detrainments decrease dramatically at the moment when convective precipitation starts to increase, suggesting intensified conversion from cloud to precipitating hydrometeors. After that, the conversion efficiency weakens, which is favorable for the formation of stratiform clouds and precipitation. Overall, this framework provides a useful tool for quantifying the characteristics and impacts of convective detrainment and for evaluating convective parameterization schemes.

articles.title: Can we define climate by means of an ensemble? A tale of time scales of convergence
articles.titleEn: Can we define climate by means of an ensemble? A tale of time scales of convergence
articles.abstract: It is not really questioned today that climate can be described in theory by an ensemble of trajectories differing in their initial conditions, which is then translated to numerical ensembles in climate models. It is also widely accepted that any evolution observed within a few decades after initialization is not yet relevant to climate. Evolution at a later stage, instead, is then used to characterize climate and its change, under the implicit assumption that slower processes do not considerably contribute to differences between ensemble members, allowing internal variability of climate to be identified with these differences. However, a careful justification for this practice is as yet lacking. In particular, a definition of climate in support of this practice is outstanding, including the identification of the kind of time scales at play through providing an argumentation for their relevance. Our study aims at filling this gap. After pointing out that the most important criterion for a definition of climate is the uniqueness of the probability measure on which the definition relies, we first recall the naive proposal to represent such a probability measure by the distribution of ensemble members that has, loosely speaking, converged to the natural probability measure of the so-called snapshot or pullback attractor of the dynamics. We then consider the time scales of convergence and refine the proposal by taking a probability measure that is conditional on the (possibly time-evolving) state of modes characterized by convergence time scales longer than the horizon of a particular study. We design an ensemble simulation initialization scheme for studying convergence time scales and uniqueness of ensembles in Earth system models.

articles.title: Convectively Coupled Equatorial Waves in a Global Storm‐Resolving Model
articles.titleEn: Convectively Coupled Equatorial Waves in a Global Storm‐Resolving Model
articles.journal: Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems
articles.abstract: We show how reducing the fall speeds of rain and ice leads to reduced biases of Convectively Coupled Equatorial Waves (CCEWs) in convection‐resolving configurations of the Icosahedral Non‐hydrostatic Model (ICON). In particular, reducing the fall speeds of rain and ice leads to stronger activity over the wavenumbers and frequencies associated with convectively coupled Kelvin waves, inertio‐gravity waves, mixed Rossby‐gravity waves, equatorial Rossby waves, and the Madden‐Julian oscillation, and to weaker activity of tropical depressions. The changes in CCEW activity are mediated by changes in the frequency of mesoscale convection profiles. Reducing the fall speeds increases the frequency of bottom‐heavy and top‐heavy mesoscale convection profiles and decreases the frequency of mid‐heavy mesoscale convection profiles. In turn, changes to the mesoscale convective profiles are reflected in the ability of the model to develop the tilt and top‐heaviness of CCEWs. Reductions in the fall speeds also increase precipitation over the warm pool region, possibly allowing for a stronger equatorial forcing of convectively coupled Kelvin waves. Our findings suggest that the representation of CCEWs within ICON agrees with their observed multiscale structure.

articles.title: Impacts of simulated coastal ocean alkalinity enhancement on the seasonal carbon cycle in European waters under a low- and a high-emission scenario
articles.titleEn: Impacts of simulated coastal ocean alkalinity enhancement on the seasonal carbon cycle in European waters under a low- and a high-emission scenario
articles.abstract: One potentially scalable method to remove CO 2 from the air is ocean alkalinity enhancement (OAE), which works to lower the ocean's CO 2 partial pressure ( p CO 2 ) and accelerate CO 2 sequestration and durable storage. This study explores how OAE might affect the seasonal carbon cycle, which plays a key role in the ocean's annual CO 2 uptake. By analysing Earth System Model simulations of OAE implemented continuously at the European coastline under low and high emissions, it was found that: (a) due to surface alkalinity retention, OAE reduces ocean p CO 2 most strongly in summer, turning the region into a year-round carbon sink; (b) the strongest air-sea CO 2 uptake enhancement takes place in winter; (c) the ocean's carbon sink is increased more strongly in SSP3-7.0 than in SSP1-2.6 due to a lower buffering capacity.

articles.title: Decadal predictions of wind, solar and compound power indicators to support the European renewable energy sector
articles.titleEn: Decadal predictions of wind, solar and compound power indicators to support the European renewable energy sector
articles.abstract: Renewable energy production is strongly influenced by climate variability and change, making the energy sector sensitive to fluctuations on decadal timescales. Decadal climate predictions, which aim to forecast climate variability over the next few years, therefore offer potential value for anticipating near-term changes in wind and solar resources and supporting climate-informed energy planning. However, the predictive skill of decadal forecasts for energy-relevant indicators remains poorly quantified, which is crucial to know the potential usability of any forecast product. This study evaluates the skill of decadal climate predictions over Europe for forecast years 1–3 using a multi-model ensemble from the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) Decadal Climate Prediction Project (DCPP). We assess three energy-relevant indicators: photovoltaic potential (PVpot), wind capacity factor (WCF), and a compound indicator describing the number of energy drought days (NED), defined as days with inefficient production from both wind and solar resources. The skill is evaluated against the ERA5 reanalysis, and the added value of the model initialization is estimated by comparing the decadal predictions against the non-initialized historical forcing simulations. PVpot exhibits the highest and most spatially homogeneous skill for annual, spring and summer aggregations, closely reflecting the high predictability of surface solar radiation. WCF shows low and spatially heterogeneous skill, consistent with the high intrinsic variability of wind. The compound NED indicator displays strong seasonal dependence: its predictability is largely controlled by solar conditions in high-radiation seasons and by wind in winter and autumn. Model initialization generally provides added value where historical simulations already show some skill, especially for PVpot, while its impact is lower for WCF. This work shows the specific seasons, regions and energy indicators for which decadal predictions can provide actionable climate information to support renewable energy applications.

articles.title: Decoded Antarctic snow accumulation history reconciles observed and modeled trends in accumulation and large-scale warming patterns
articles.titleEn: Decoded Antarctic snow accumulation history reconciles observed and modeled trends in accumulation and large-scale warming patterns
articles.abstract: Increased snow accumulation on the Antarctic Ice Sheet mitigated global sea level rise by ∼ 11 mm during 1901–2000 according to ice core reconstructions. However, in the most recent 40 years of more intense observation and warming, the trend in the Antarctic-wide accumulation rate has been negligible. We attribute these trends by evaluating Earth system model experiments in comparison with dynamically consistent reconstructions of surface climate. Single-forcing experiments reveal that rising concentrations of greenhouse gases (GHGs) have been the underlying driver of increased accumulation, yet acting alone would have caused twice the observed accumulation-related sea level mitigation during 1901–2000. Aerosol-driven cooling partially compensates this overprediction, but the reconstructions provide evidence that poorly modeled processes can explain observation-model trend discrepancies. In particular, these data support a hypothesis that high-latitude winds have been working together with ice-shelf meltwater fluxes to dampen Southern Ocean surface warming and suppress the GHG-driven accumulation increase since the initiation of West Antarctic ice shelf thinning in the mid-20th Century. The wind pattern associated with strengthening of the Southern Hemisphere westerlies and deepening of the Amundsen Sea Low distributes accumulation unevenly across the continent in an orographic pattern that is consistent across models and the reconstructions. In reconstructions, these same wind and accumulation patterns are associated with muted surface warming across the eastern Pacific and Southern Ocean, a pattern not captured in climate projections including the all-forcings large ensemble studied here. However, the westerly wind history constrained by paleoclimate data assimilation largely reconciles differences between the model's ensemble-mean response and the observed world for both Antarctic-wide accumulation and large-scale warming patterns. Although the large ensemble simulates similar wind histories to the real one – driven by internal variability and anthropogenic forcing – its corresponding responses in SSTs and Antarctic-wide snow accumulation are decoupled from the wind. We discuss how this significant observation-model discrepancy, which has implications for projecting regional climate change, likely arises from omitted meltwater forcing and/or resolution limitations. As a component of the sea level budget and a gauge of the magnitude and spatial pattern of climate change, Antarctic snow accumulation is a critical target for models to replicate.

articles.title: Regional contrasts of ecosystem productivity sensitivity to atmospheric CO 2 growth across East Asia
articles.titleEn: Regional contrasts of ecosystem productivity sensitivity to atmospheric CO 2 growth across East Asia
articles.abstract: Elevated global atmospheric CO 2 intensifies the complexity of climate variability and ecosystem productivity, and its impact on the terrestrial carbon cycle remains unclear. Using twelve Dynamic Global Vegetation Models (DGVMs) in Trends in land carbon cycle datasets and Global Carbon Budget dataset, we quantified the sensitivity of ecosystem productivity-defined as the rate of change in productivity with global atmospheric CO 2 growth rate-in East Asia from 1959 to 2023. Most DGVMs showed net ecosystem production sensitivity as negative, implying an intensification of the inverse relationship with atmospheric CO 2 growth. By separating East Asia into the monsoon and non-monsoon regions, we examined the temporal changes in gross primary productivity sensitivity, which has been decreasing in both regions since the late 1990s. These productivity responses were primarily controlled by soil moisture sensitivity in the non-monsoon region, whereas photosynthetically active radiation emerged as the key factor in the monsoon region. Furthermore, differences in vegetation structure between the monsoon and non-monsoon regions may contribute to regional differences in the mechanisms associated with vegetation productivity responses to atmospheric CO 2 growth. By considering regional climate systems and vegetation characteristics, this study highlights that environmental and structural differences influence the ecosystem response to atmospheric CO 2 growth. Ultimately, our findings suggest that considering regionally distinct climate-vegetation feedbacks is essential for improving the accuracy of global carbon cycle projections under future climate change.

articles.title: Assessing Earth system responses in mitigation scenarios with activity-driven simulation of carbon dioxide removal
articles.titleEn: Assessing Earth system responses in mitigation scenarios with activity-driven simulation of carbon dioxide removal
articles.abstract: Assessing Earth system responses arising from carbon dioxide removal (CDR) requires developing and simulating pairs of scenarios – a mitigation scenario with deployment of CDR and a corresponding no-CDR baseline. The latter describes a world where no CDR is deployed, such that net carbon emissions are higher and a given temperature target may be missed. While over the past years a rich literature on mitigation scenarios with CDR has been emerging, no-CDR baselines have mostly been explored in stylized Earth system model (ESM) experiments. In such simulations, a no-CDR baseline simply assumes that CDR is “switched off”, while socio-economic constraints are not considered. However, the deployment of CDR in mitigation scenarios, created by integrated assessment models (IAMs), is embedded in a consistent socio-economic description of plausible futures, and disallowing CDR may affect climate drivers due to changes in the energy system and in land-use dynamics. Particularly, when moving towards an activity-driven representation of CDR in emission-driven ESMs, where the activity that draws down CO 2 from the atmosphere is explicitly modelled, the creation of no-CDR baselines comes with challenges and trade-offs. Here, we conceptualize a framework for emission-driven ESM simulations of IAM scenarios that allows us to determine carbon-cycle feedbacks and biogeophysical effects of CDR deployment using no-CDR baselines. We show that different options exist for the creation of no-CDR baselines, which offer different insights and have their specific advantages and limitations. We also demonstrate that internal variability of the climate system inherently limits our ability to detect the small signals related to CDR deployment and its feedbacks. Hence, unless a sufficiently large initial conditions ensemble is employed, stylized modelling approaches may remain preferable for some applications, e.g., the quantification of regional biogeophysical effects of CDR deployment. Both, the efficiency of CDR (defined as CO 2 removed per unit of resources employed) as well as related carbon-cycle feedbacks and biogeophysical effects are expected to be scenario- and model-dependent. Our simulation design of concentration- and emission-driven no-CDR baselines, together with an improved representation of CDR in the IAM – ESM modelling chain, opens an avenue towards estimating CDR efficiencies and their uncertainties under various future scenarios in upcoming model intercomparison activities.
